posts.title: Spark-to-Paper: An AI That Runs Its Own Research Loop
posts.subtitle: Thirteen composable skills turn a raw idea into a submittable paper, end to end.
posts.summary: Spark-to-Paper (arXiv:2608.11924) implements end-to-end research paper generation as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant. It separates deterministic checks from model judgment and specifies evidence requirements before experiments run, then bounds a documented failure mode called the Self-Refutation Loop where iterative self-critique talks the model out of correct findings.

slides.title: Can an AI Run Its Own Research Loop?
slides.body: A new system turns a one-line research idea into a full paper draft, without a bespoke agent platform.
bullets: Thirteen composable skills
Runs inside an existing coding assistant
Posted to arXiv Aug 12, 2026

slides.title: Writing a Paper Is Not One Task, It's Ten
slides.body: Turning an idea into a paper means retrieving literature, designing and running experiments, revising claims to match evidence, producing figures, and staying consistent across a long generation process — all before a word of the final draft is 'done'.
bullets: A single long LLM call collapses these into one blob and drifts
Claims and figures easily go out of sync with what was actually measured
Long generation runs compound small errors into large ones

slides.title: Thirteen Skills, Not One Giant Agent
slides.body: Spark-to-Paper is implemented as thirteen composable skills inside an existing coding assistant — no separate orchestration platform required.
bullets: Deterministic, checkable operations (retrieval, running code, checking a figure against its data) are split from model judgment calls
Experiment planning is separated from reporting: success criteria are written down before results are observed
That ordering is the whole trick — it blocks after-the-fact rationalization of whatever the experiment happened to produce

slides.title: The Self-Refutation Loop
slides.body: A documented failure mode: when a model repeatedly critiques its own claims, it can spiral — talking itself out of a correct finding, or into an incorrect one, on each pass.
bullets: Self-critique alone doesn't converge to truth, it converges to whatever the last critique argued
Spark-to-Paper bounds the loop with deterministic integrity checks that anchor revisions back to measured evidence
Bounding it isn't eliminating it — see the pitfalls slide

slides.title: From a One-Line Hypothesis to a Draft Section
slides.body: A researcher inputs: 'Does the order of examples in a prompt affect retrieval accuracy?' The system doesn't just answer — it works the loop.
bullets: Retrieval skill pulls related prior work before any experiment is designed
Planning skill locks in a success metric and a threshold up front
Execution skill runs the actual test and logs raw output
Reporting skill revises the claim to match what was measured — not what was hoped for — then generates the figure from the same run

slides.title: Who Owns Each Step

rows: Judging whether evidence supports a claim
Checking a figure matches its underlying data
Revising the narrative to fit results
Model judgment, bounded by the anti-refutation checks

slides.title: Where This Breaks
slides.body: This is scaffolding for the writing-and-evidencing loop, not a substitute for a good research question.
bullets: Inherits the limits of the underlying coding assistant it runs inside (context handling, tool errors)
The Self-Refutation Loop is bounded, not solved — it's a named risk to watch for, not a guarantee
A weak or trivial starting hypothesis still produces a weak paper, just a fluently-written one
Doesn't replace peer review or domain expertise on whether the question was worth asking

slides.title: The Real Insight Isn't 'AI Writes Papers'
slides.body: It's the ordering discipline: decide what would count as evidence before you see the results, and keep deterministic checks between the model and its own claims.
bullets: Separate what can be checked by code from what needs judgment
Lock success criteria in before running the experiment
Bound self-critique loops instead of trusting them to converge on their own

questions.prompt: What does the 'Self-Refutation Loop' describe in Spark-to-Paper?
options: A security exploit where the agent leaks training data
A failure mode where repeated self-critique spirals the model away from a correct finding
A reinforcement learning training algorithm
A formatting bug in generated LaTeX
questions.explanation: It's a named failure mode of iterative self-critique: without an anchor, each critique pass can push the model further from — not closer to — the correct claim. Spark-to-Paper bounds it with deterministic integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Why does the system lock in success criteria before running an experiment?
options: To make the experiment run faster
It's an arXiv submission requirement
To prevent revising the claim after seeing results — i.e. cherry-picking or rationalizing
To reduce the number of API calls needed
questions.explanation: Committing to what counts as evidence before observing outcomes is the core discipline: it blocks the common failure of quietly reshaping a claim to fit whatever result actually came out.

questions.prompt: How is Spark-to-Paper architected?
options: As a standalone multi-agent orchestration platform
As a single fine-tuned model checkpoint
As thirteen composable skills running inside an existing coding assistant
As a browser extension for Google Docs
questions.explanation: No bespoke agent platform — the thirteen skills are composable pieces that plug into a coding assistant that already exists, which is part of why the approach is notable.

references.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill (arXiv:2608.11924)

posts.title: Grok 4.6: SpaceXAI's First Flagship After the Merger
posts.subtitle: xAI is gone — fully absorbed into SpaceX — and its first post-merger model trades raw IQ for agentic stamina.
posts.summary: SpaceXAI (the rebrand of xAI after its full merger into SpaceX) shipped Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, just 35 days after Grok 4.5. It scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — matching GPT-5.6 Sol — and is tuned for long-running agentic work: it finishes long knowledge-work tasks in about half the turns Claude Opus 5 needs, at $0.84 per task, though it still trails Opus 5 on raw agentic Elo.

slides.title: Grok Just Got a New Parent Company
slides.body: The first flagship model released since xAI was fully folded into SpaceX and renamed SpaceXAI.
bullets: Released August 12, 2026
35 days after Grok 4.5
Tuned for long-running agents, not a ground-up rebuild

slides.title: Why the Rebrand Is Part of the Story
slides.body: This isn't a naming gimmick — it's a real corporate restructuring that changes who ships and supports Grok going forward.
bullets: SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock deal in February 2026
xAI was dissolved as a standalone company and fully integrated into SpaceX by July 2026
Grok models, the X platform, and related AI infrastructure now sit under the SpaceXAI umbrella inside SpaceX

slides.title: What Actually Changed in 4.6
slides.body: The architecture didn't get a ground-up rewrite — the training recipe and target use case did.
bullets: Context window unchanged from Grok 4.5: 500,000 tokens
Training added a longer supplemental run using Grok-4.5-regenerated SFT trajectories, filtered by model-based checks
Followed by agentic reinforcement learning targeted at long-running agent tasks and interactive/visual work

slides.title: The Numbers

rows: 61 — up 5 points from Grok 4.5, matches GPT-5.6 Sol, one point behind Claude Fable 5
Elo 1577 on debut — behind Claude Opus 5
~53 turns to finish a task vs. Opus 5's ~103, at $0.84/task

slides.title: A Long-Horizon Task, Turn by Turn
slides.body: AA-Briefcase scores agents on real long-horizon knowledge-work projects — the kind that take dozens of tool calls, not a single prompt-response.
bullets: Grok 4.6 wraps the same class of task in roughly half the turns Claude Opus 5 needs
At $0.84 per completed task, it's built to be cheap to run at that pace
But Opus 5 still finishes with a higher completion-quality Elo — Grok 4.6 is faster and cheaper, not (yet) better on this benchmark

slides.title: Fast and Cheap Isn't the Same as Ahead
slides.body: Read the benchmarks as a tradeoff, not a crown.
bullets: Matches GPT-5.6 Sol on raw intelligence, trails Claude Fable 5 by a point — not the outright smartest model on the board
Wins on cost and turn-efficiency for agentic work, not on peak agentic quality where Opus 5 still leads
A 35-day release cadence plus a same-quarter full corporate absorption into SpaceX is fast — worth watching whether safety review depth keeps pace with release speed

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: xAI no longer exists as a standalone company — it's SpaceXAI, fully inside SpaceX
Grok 4.6 ties GPT-5.6 Sol on raw intelligence and is priced/tuned for long agentic runs
It's the efficiency pick for long-horizon agent tasks, not the peak-quality pick — that's still Claude Opus 5 by this benchmark

options: xAI completed an independent IPO
xAI was fully merged into SpaceX and rebranded SpaceXAI
xAI was acquired by a rival AI lab
Grok's weights were open-sourced
questions.explanation: SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026 and fully absorbed it by July 2026, renaming the AI effort SpaceXAI — Grok 4.6 is the first flagship model released under that name.

Roughly matches it, both at 61
Far ahead
It wasn't benchmarked against it

options: Higher accuracy but far slower per task
Finishes tasks in fewer turns at lower cost, but trails Claude Opus 5's completion-quality Elo
It cannot handle multi-step agentic tasks at all
It requires no context window limit

posts.title: Context Rot: Why Bigger Windows Don't Mean Better Recall
posts.subtitle: Every frontier model tested degrades as input grows, often well before it hits the documented limit.
posts.summary: Context rot is the well-documented tendency of LLMs to answer less reliably as input length grows, even far short of their advertised context limit. Chroma's 2025 study found this in all 18 frontier models tested, and earlier work ('Lost in the Middle') showed accuracy drops over 30% when a key fact sits mid-prompt instead of at the start or end. Counterintuitively, well-structured input can degrade attention more than shuffled input. The practical fix is retrieving a narrow, relevant slice of context rather than trusting a large window to hold everything reliably.

slides.title: The Context Window Lied to You
slides.body: A 200K-token window doesn't mean 200K tokens of reliable recall.
bullets: 18 frontier models tested, all degrade
Serious accuracy loss can appear at just 25% of the stated limit
Chroma Research, July 2025

slides.title: More Tokens, Worse Answers
slides.body: 'Context rot' names a specific finding: accuracy drops non-uniformly as input length grows — present at every length increment tested, in every model tested.
bullets: Contradicts the assumption that a bigger window means it's safe to just paste everything in
A 200K-token window can show serious accuracy loss with only ~50K tokens of actual input
GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5 were among the models exhibiting it

slides.title: Lost in the Middle
slides.body: Liu et al. (TACL 2024) found a U-shaped position effect on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks.
bullets: Accuracy is highest when the relevant fact sits at the very start or end of the prompt
Accuracy drops by more than 30% when that same fact is buried in the middle
Replicated across six model families: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, Claude 1.3, LongChat-13B, MPT-30B, Cohere Command

slides.title: The Counterintuitive Part
slides.body: You'd expect well-organized, coherent input to help a model find what it needs. Chroma found the opposite at scale.
bullets: Coherent, well-structured input degraded attention MORE than shuffled, incoherent input
Structure that helps a human reader doesn't reliably help a transformer's attention over long context
It's a reminder that human reading intuitions don't automatically transfer to how these models actually attend

slides.title: Debugging a 90K-Token System Prompt
slides.body: An engineer stuffs a 90K-token onboarding doc plus tool specs into a system prompt, with the one critical safety instruction placed in the middle.
bullets: The agent silently ignores that instruction on a meaningful fraction of runs
Not because the instruction is wrong — because of where it sits in the prompt
Moving the same instruction to the very start (or repeating it at the end) measurably improves adherence

slides.title: Where Accuracy Actually Holds

headers: What Chroma / Liu et al. Observed
rows: Input well under the stated context limit
Input around ~25% of the stated window (e.g. 50K of 200K)
Serious accuracy loss can already appear
Key fact placed in the middle vs. start/end
Accuracy drops over 30% (Lost in the Middle)
Structured input can degrade attention more, not less

slides.title: So What Do You Actually Do?
slides.body: Treat a large context window as capacity, not as a guarantee of recall.
bullets: Don't paste an entire corpus just because the window fits it — retrieve the relevant 50K-200K tokens first, then reason over that
Put the most critical instruction at the very start or end of a long prompt, never buried in the middle
Test your prompts at the lengths you'll actually run in production, not just at the documented maximum

slides.title: What to Remember
bullets: Context rot is universal across frontier models, not a quirk of one lab's model
Position matters as much as presence — start/end beats middle by a wide margin
Retrieval-then-reason beats dump-everything-in-the-window, even when the window technically fits it all

questions.prompt: What did Chroma's 2025 'Context Rot' study find across the 18 models it tested?
options: None of the models degraded with longer input
Every model degrades non-uniformly as input grows, often well before its documented limit
Only open-source models showed degradation
Degradation only appears above 1 million tokens
questions.explanation: The degradation showed up in all 18 frontier models tested, at every input-length increment — including well-known models like GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4, and Gemini 2.5.

questions.prompt: According to 'Lost in the Middle,' where should the most important fact in a long prompt go for best recall?
options: Exactly in the middle
At the very start or end of the context
It doesn't matter
Split evenly throughout the prompt
questions.explanation: Liu et al. found a U-shaped curve: accuracy is highest when key information sits at the start or end, and drops over 30% when it's buried in the middle.

questions.prompt: What was the counterintuitive finding about well-structured, coherent input?
options: It always improves model performance
It can degrade attention more than shuffled, incoherent input at scale
It has no measurable effect
It only matters for code inputs
questions.explanation: Chroma found structured input can hurt long-context attention more than shuffled input — a case where human-reading intuition doesn't predict model behavior.

references.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance — Chroma Research
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (Liu et al., TACL 2024)

posts.title: Test-Time Capability Transfer: Harnesses, Not Fine-Tuning
posts.subtitle: A stronger model writes deterministic scaffolding that nearly doubles a weaker model's accuracy — no gradient update in sight.
posts.summary: Salesforce AI Research and UIUC show that a strong 'builder' model can write a deterministic inference-time harness — code, routing, and format rules — that lets a much weaker 'target' model solve tasks it otherwise fails, without touching a single weight. On four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, average target accuracy went from 0.49 to 0.91.

slides.title: One Model Builds the Harness, Another Runs It
slides.body: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses — Salesforce AI Research + UIUC, arXiv:2608.12307, Aug 12 2026.
bullets: No fine-tuning, no distillation, no new weights
Capability moves through scaffolding, not parameters

slides.title: Weak Models Don't Fail Randomly — They Fail Predictably
slides.body: A small or cheap model missing a benchmark usually isn't 'less intelligent' in a fuzzy sense — it mis-formats answers, skips reasoning steps, or picks the wrong sub-strategy in consistent, fixable ways.
bullets: The obvious fixes — use a bigger model, or fine-tune the small one — cost money, data, or both
The paper asks: can a strong model fix a weak model's *process* instead of its *weights*?

slides.title: The Builder Writes Code, Routing Rules, and Format Contracts
slides.body: A strong 'builder' model is given the task family and a small validation slice, then iteratively authors a harness that wraps the weak 'target' model at inference time.
bullets: Harness = deterministic code + benchmark-specific routing + strict answer-format enforcement
Builder uses only 5% of the data as a validation set, refining the harness over multiple rounds
Once locked, the harness runs on the full test set — the target model's weights never change

slides.title: Example: A Weak Model Doing Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
slides.body: On a Theory-of-Mind benchmark (inferring what one character knows vs. another), the raw target model reasons inconsistently and sometimes answers in the wrong format entirely.
bullets: The harness intercepts the model's output, routes ambiguous cases to a deterministic sub-solver, and rejects/retries malformed answers
The target model still does the 'thinking' — the harness just stops its process errors from becoming task failures

slides.title: Nearly Double the Accuracy, Zero Parameter Updates
slides.body: Averaged across four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks:

slides.title: Where the Gains Actually Come From
slides.body: The paper is explicit about the mechanism — it isn't 'the model reasons more.'
bullets: Gains come from offloading unstable reasoning into deterministic code, not from longer chains of thought or more sampling
The weakest target models benefit the most — there's more process-error to remove
This makes it closer to a compiler pass over the model's behavior than a training technique

slides.title: When This Doesn't Help
slides.body: The setup has real constraints worth knowing before you reach for it.
bullets: You need a strong builder model available at authoring time — that's a real cost, even if it's paid once
Validated only on Theory-of-Mind benchmarks with clear, checkable structure; open-ended generation tasks may not have an equivalent 'deterministic harness' to write
A harness tuned tightly to a benchmark's format risks overfitting to that benchmark rather than the underlying skill

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Capability can transfer at test time through scaffolding, not just through weights
Deterministic code + routing + format enforcement fixed more errors than 'reason harder' would have
Cheap local models plus a well-built harness can close a surprising amount of the gap to bigger models

questions.prompt: In the paper's setup, what actually changes about the weak 'target' model?
options: Its weights are fine-tuned on the validation slice
Nothing — it's wrapped by an inference-time harness built by a stronger model
It's distilled into a smaller architecture
It's replaced by the builder model at test time
questions.explanation: The target model's parameters are never touched. All the gain comes from an external harness — code, routing, format rules — that the builder model authors around it.

questions.prompt: Where do most of the accuracy gains come from, according to the paper?
options: Encouraging the target model to sample more responses and vote
Giving the target model a longer chain-of-thought budget
Offloading unstable reasoning into deterministic code, routing, and format enforcement
Replacing the target model's tokenizer
questions.explanation: The authors are explicit that gains come from structural fixes — deterministic code and strict formatting — not from the target model reasoning more extensively or sampling more broadly.

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation of this approach highlighted by its setup?
options: It requires the target model's training data
It requires a strong builder model to author the harness, and was validated on structured Theory-of-Mind tasks specifically
It only works if both models have the same architecture
It cannot be evaluated on a held-out test set
questions.explanation: Authoring the harness needs a capable builder model, and the demonstrated results are on four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks with checkable structure — it's not yet shown to generalize to open-ended generation tasks.

references.title: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses (arXiv:2608.12307)

posts.title: Qwen3.8-27B: A 27B Open Model That Runs on One GPU
posts.subtitle: Apache 2.0, 262K native context, native vision — and it beats Opus 4.6 Max on exactly one of five cited benchmarks.
posts.summary: Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced Qwen3.8-27B on Aug 14, 2026: a dense 27B multimodal model under Apache 2.0 with 262K native context and a reasoning-effort dial, runnable on a single consumer GPU. It jumps sharply over its own predecessor and edges out Claude Opus 4.6 Max on one benchmark — but trails it clearly on most others.

slides.title: A Frontier-Adjacent Model You Can Run Locally
slides.body: Qwen3.8-27B — Alibaba Qwen, released Aug 14, 2026, Apache 2.0 license.
bullets: 27B dense parameters, native multimodal
#1 trending on Hugging Face within days, 3M+ downloads

slides.title: Open Models Usually Trade Capability for Size
slides.body: The most capable open-weight models have generally meant either mixture-of-experts giants or dense models too large for a single consumer GPU — pushing serious local use out of reach for most developers.
bullets: Running a frontier-adjacent open model at home usually meant multi-GPU setups or heavy quantization
Qwen3.8-27B targets that gap directly: strong benchmarks at a size that fits ~16-17GB of VRAM

slides.title: Dense 27B, 262K Context, a Reasoning Dial
slides.body: Rather than a mixture-of-experts design, Qwen3.8-27B is a dense multimodal model with a few notable specs.
bullets: 262,144-token native context, extendable to 1M tokens via YaRN
Native image and video understanding built in, not bolted on
A reasoning_effort parameter to trade latency/cost against answer quality per request
Weights released on Hugging Face and ModelScope under Apache 2.0

slides.title: A Large Jump Over Its Own Predecessor
slides.body: Alibaba's own benchmark comparisons show the biggest gains are relative to the prior Qwen generation, not necessarily against frontier proprietary models:

slides.title: Example: An Agentic Coding Task on a Single GPU
slides.body: A developer points Qwen3.8-27B at a repo through an agent harness for a multi-file coding task, running entirely on one consumer-grade GPU (~16-17GB).
bullets: The reasoning_effort dial lets them run cheap/fast for simple edits, then turn it up for a gnarly refactor
262K native context means most repos' relevant files fit without aggressive chunking

slides.title: The 'Beats Opus 4.6 Max' Headline Needs a Footnote
slides.body: Coverage highlighting Qwen3.8-27B beating Claude Opus 4.6 Max is accurate for exactly one benchmark, not a general claim.
bullets: On SWE-bench Pro, Qwen3.8-27B scores 61.7 vs. a cited 53.4 for Opus 4.6 Max — but that Opus figure is imported from Anthropic's own report, not rerun under Qwen's harness, so it isn't a fully controlled comparison
On HLE, Qwen3.8-27B trails clearly: 30.8 vs. 40.0 for Opus 4.6 Max
Some cited benchmarks (QwenSWEBench, CoWorkBench, RecreationBench) are Qwen's own, and don't yet have the external auditability of a mature public suite

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A genuinely strong open-weight jump for a size that fits one GPU — the predecessor-vs-new-version gains are the most solid numbers here
Treat 'beats a frontier proprietary model' claims benchmark-by-benchmark, not as a blanket statement
262K native context and a reasoning-effort dial make it a practical pick for local agentic workloads, not just a benchmark chart

questions.prompt: What architecture choice does Qwen3.8-27B make, compared to many other large open models?
options: It's a sparse mixture-of-experts model
It's a dense model, not mixture-of-experts
It's a retrieval-augmented model with no parameters of its own
It uses a diffusion-based text decoder
questions.explanation: Qwen3.8-27B is dense — all 27B parameters activate per token — which is part of why it fits on a single consumer GPU at this parameter count.

questions.prompt: On which cited benchmark does Qwen3.8-27B actually score above Claude Opus 4.6 Max?
options: HLE
SWE-bench Pro
All five cited benchmarks
None — it trails on every benchmark
questions.explanation: It scores 61.7 vs. a cited 53.4 on SWE-bench Pro — though that Opus figure is imported rather than rerun, so the comparison isn't fully controlled. It trails clearly on HLE (30.8 vs. 40.0).

questions.prompt: What lets Qwen3.8-27B extend context beyond its native 262,144 tokens?
options: Retrieval-augmented generation
A second, smaller summarizer model
YaRN-based context extension, up to 1M tokens
It cannot exceed its native context
questions.explanation: The model's native context is 262,144 tokens, extendable to 1M tokens via YaRN, a rotary-position-embedding scaling technique.

posts.title: MCP Resources: Context the App Attaches, Not the Model
posts.subtitle: The quiet MCP primitive: application-controlled data with URIs, push subscriptions, and — as of the 2026-07-28 spec — HTTP-style cache hints.
posts.summary: MCP splits context into three primitives by who decides: Tools are model-controlled, Prompts are user-controlled, and Resources are application-controlled. Resources give servers a way to expose addressable data — files, rows, active documents — that the host can attach, subscribe to, and now cache using spec-defined hints, without spending a model turn on a tool call.

slides.title: The MCP Primitive That Isn't a Tool Call
slides.body: Every MCP server can expose Tools, Prompts, and Resources. Resources are the one most tutorials skip — and the one that saves the most tokens.
bullets: Application-controlled, not model-controlled
Addressable by URI, readable on demand or by subscription

slides.title: Tools Are the Wrong Shape for 'Just Attach This File'
slides.body: If the host already knows the user has a file open, a database row selected, or a document active, routing that data through a tool call is wasteful.
bullets: A tool call spends a model turn deciding to call a tool, then another turn processing the result
The app already knows what context it wants attached — the model shouldn't have to ask for it

slides.title: Three Primitives, Three Different Controllers
slides.body: MCP's context surface splits cleanly by who decides it gets used:
bullets: Tools — model-controlled: the LLM decides when to call them, based on its own reasoning
Prompts — user-controlled: reusable templates the human explicitly selects (e.g. a slash command)
Resources — application-controlled: the host decides what to attach, list, or subscribe to

slides.title: resources/list and resources/read
slides.body: A server that supports resources responds to resources/list with the resources currently available, and to resources/read with their content.
bullets: Each resource has a URI (any scheme — file://, postgres://, custom), a name, a description, and a mimeType
Content comes back as text or a base64-encoded blob, matched to the mimeType
The host decides which listed resources to actually attach to the model's context — listing isn't attaching

slides.title: Subscriptions Turn Polling Into Push
slides.body: Servers declare a resources capability that can include listChanged and subscribe support.
bullets: resources/subscribe on a URI means the host gets notifications/resources/updated when that resource changes — no polling loop needed
notifications/resources/list_changed fires when the *set* of available resources changes (a file created, a table added)
This is what makes 'the model has live awareness of these three open files' cheap to implement

slides.title: Example: An IDE Exposing Open Tabs as Resources
slides.body: An IDE's MCP server exposes each open editor tab as a resource (file:///path/to/file.ts) rather than requiring the model to call a 'read_file' tool for each one.
bullets: The host subscribes to the active tab's URI
When the user edits and saves, the server pushes notifications/resources/updated — the host re-reads and refreshes the model's context automatically
No tool call, no extra model turn, no stale file content

slides.title: Tools vs. Resources vs. Prompts

rows: Take an action, fetch data on demand
Attach known context: files, rows, docs

slides.title: New in the 2026-07-28 Spec: Cache Hints
slides.body: resources/list and resources/read results can now carry ttlMs and cacheScope fields, modeled directly on HTTP Cache-Control.
bullets: A client can skip re-reading a resource it already has, until the ttlMs expires
cacheScope indicates whether that cached copy is safe to reuse across sessions or only within one
This matters for resources that rarely change (a schema) vs. ones that change constantly (an open file)

slides.title: When a Resource Is the Wrong Choice
slides.body: Resources aren't a universal replacement for tools.
bullets: If the model needs to decide *what* to fetch based on its own reasoning (search a query, pick a record), that's a Tool's job, not a Resource
The resources capability, including subscribe, is optional — plenty of clients don't support it yet, so don't design around push-only assumptions
Attaching a resource still consumes context window budget once it's in — a cache hint saves a re-fetch, not the tokens themselves

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Resources are for context the application already knows it wants attached — Tools are for context the model decides it needs
Subscriptions replace polling: subscribe once, get notified on change
The 2026-07-28 spec added HTTP-style cache hints (ttlMs, cacheScope) to cut redundant re-reads

questions.prompt: Who decides which Resources actually get attached to the model's context?
options: The model, via a tool call
The application/host
The end user, via a slash command
The MCP server, automatically, with no host involvement
questions.explanation: Resources are application-controlled: the host lists and reads them, then decides what to attach. This is the key distinction from Tools, which the model itself decides to invoke.

questions.prompt: How does an MCP client avoid polling a resource for changes?
options: It re-reads the resource on every model turn
It calls resources/subscribe on the URI and receives notifications/resources/updated when it changes
It's not possible — MCP has no notification mechanism
It relies on the model to ask periodically
questions.explanation: A server that declares subscribe support lets clients subscribe to a specific resource URI and get pushed notifications/resources/updated events instead of polling.

questions.prompt: What did the 2026-07-28 MCP spec add to resources/list and resources/read results?

posts.title: Quantization: Same Model, a Quarter of the Memory
posts.subtitle: How GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF squeeze 16-bit weights into 4 bits without wrecking the model.
posts.summary: Quantization maps a model's 16-bit weights to lower-precision integers (INT8, INT4) to cut memory and speed up inference. Methods like GPTQ and AWQ differ in which weights they protect and how they correct for the introduced error, and picking the right one is a tradeoff between size, speed, and quality.

slides.title: A 70B Model Doesn't Have to Mean 140GB of VRAM
slides.body: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, shrinking memory and often speeding up inference — for a small, controllable hit to accuracy.

slides.title: Every Parameter Costs Bytes, and Big Models Have Billions of Them
bullets: FP32 stores each weight in 4 bytes, FP16/BF16 in 2 — a 7B-parameter model in FP16 needs roughly 14GB just for weights.
A 70B model in FP16 needs roughly 140GB — more VRAM than a single high-end GPU has, forcing multi-GPU setups just to load it.
Decoding is usually memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound — smaller weights mean less data to move per generated token.
The KV cache adds more memory pressure on top of the weights, so shrinking weight size directly buys headroom for longer contexts.

slides.title: Quantization Maps Each Weight to a Small Integer Plus a Scale
slides.body: Instead of storing a 16-bit float, you store a low-bit integer and a per-group scale (and sometimes a zero-point) that maps it back to an approximate float value.
bullets: INT8 uses 1 byte/weight, INT4 uses 0.5 byte — an INT4 model is roughly a quarter the size of its FP16 original.
Weights are grouped (e.g. 128 per group) so each group gets its own scale factor, keeping the mapping precise despite the low bit count.
Weight-only quantization keeps activations in higher precision (simpler, less accuracy loss); weight+activation quantization compresses both for extra speed but is harder to get right.
Quantization can happen after training (PTQ — cheap, minutes to hours) or during training (QAT — expensive, but better quality at very low bit-widths).

slides.title: GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF Disagree on What to Protect
bullets: GPTQ quantizes layer by layer, using approximate second-order (Hessian) information to adjust remaining weights and cancel out the error each rounding step introduces.
AWQ observes that a small fraction of weight channels dominate activation magnitude, and protects exactly those channels with per-channel scaling instead of treating every weight equally.
GGUF (llama.cpp) uses mixed 'k-quant' block schemes tuned for CPU and edge inference, trading a bit more size for simple, dependency-free deployment.
NF4 (used in QLoRA) is a 4-bit format shaped to match the bell-curve distribution of neural network weights, not a plain linear integer grid.

slides.title: Fitting an 8B-Class Model on a Single Consumer GPU
slides.body: An 8B-parameter model in FP16 needs about 16GB — already tight on a 16GB card once KV cache and activations are added. Quantized to INT4, the weights drop to roughly 4-5GB.
bullets: That smaller footprint leaves room for a much larger KV cache, so the same GPU now handles longer conversations, not just a smaller model.
On a laptop with 8-16GB of unified memory, INT4 is often the difference between a model loading at all and not fitting in memory.
4-bit GPTQ/AWQ on a 7-8B model typically stays close to FP16 quality on standard benchmarks, while pushing further to 2-bit causes a visible, noticeable drop.
Serving stacks each support a different subset of formats — vLLM and TGI favor GPTQ/AWQ, llama.cpp favors GGUF — so the quantization method also picks your deployment stack.

slides.title: Quantization Error Doesn't Show Up Evenly
bullets: Outlier weights and activations, common in larger models, are hardest to represent in low bits — naive rounding can wreck exactly the values that matter most.
Calibration-based methods (GPTQ, AWQ) need a small representative dataset; a mismatched calibration set can quietly degrade quality on domains it never saw.
Rounding error compounds across layers and across generation steps, so quantization tends to hurt long chain-of-thought and multi-step reasoning more than single-turn answers.
Not every quantized format has a fast kernel on every GPU — a format that looks great on paper can still run slower than FP16 without an optimized kernel for it.

slides.title: Pick the Bit-Width the Deployment Target Actually Needs
bullets: INT8 is close to a free lunch: half the memory of FP16, minimal quality loss — a good default when you're not memory-constrained.
INT4 (GPTQ/AWQ/NF4) is the sweet spot for running large models on limited hardware, at the cost of a small, usually acceptable quality dip.
Below 4-bit, quality loss becomes visible fast — reserve 2-3 bit for cases where fitting the model at all matters more than peak accuracy.
Match the format to the serving stack (vLLM/TGI want GPTQ or AWQ; llama.cpp wants GGUF) before optimizing anything else.

questions.prompt: What's the main memory saving from moving a model's weights from FP16 to INT4?
options: No change — only compute speed improves
Weights shrink to roughly a quarter of the FP16 size
Weights double in size
Only the KV cache shrinks, not the weights
questions.explanation: FP16 uses 2 bytes per weight and INT4 uses 0.5 bytes — a 4x reduction, which is why a 70B model's weight memory can shrink from roughly 140GB toward roughly 35GB.

questions.prompt: What does AWQ specifically protect that naive rounding would damage?
options: Every weight equally, via one global scale
The small fraction of weight channels with the largest activation magnitude
Only the first layer of the network
The KV cache values
questions.explanation: AWQ identifies that a small percentage of weight channels dominate activation magnitude and applies per-channel scaling to protect exactly those channels, rather than treating all weights the same.

questions.prompt: Why can quantization hurt multi-step reasoning more than single-turn answers?
options: It doesn't — reasoning is unaffected by quantization
Rounding error introduced at each layer and each generation step compounds over a longer chain of steps
Quantized models can't do reasoning at all
Multi-step reasoning always requires FP32 precision
questions.explanation: Small per-step rounding errors accumulate — a chain-of-thought with many steps has more opportunities for compounding drift than a single-turn factual answer.

posts.title: Plan-and-Execute: Separating Planning From Acting
posts.subtitle: Why some agents draft the whole itinerary first instead of deciding one step at a time.
posts.summary: Plan-and-Execute splits an agent into a Planner that decomposes a goal into an ordered task list with one LLM call, and an Executor that works through the steps — only looping back to a Replanner when something fails or the world changes. It trades ReAct's step-by-step adaptability for lower cost and a global view of the task, but a stale plan can silently steer execution off course.

slides.title: Draft the Whole Plan, Then Execute It
slides.body: Instead of deciding one step at a time like ReAct, a Planner call lays out the entire ordered task list up front — execution then mostly just follows it.

slides.title: Step-by-Step Reasoning Gets Expensive and Loses the Plot
slides.body: In an interleaved loop like ReAct, every single step re-sends the full trajectory so far and asks the model to decide only the next move.
bullets: Token cost grows with every step, since the whole thought/action/observation history is resent each turn
The model only ever sees 'what's next', never the full shape of the task — it can wander down locally-reasonable but globally wrong paths
Independent sub-steps can't be parallelized, because each one waits on a fresh reasoning turn

slides.title: Planner, Executor, Replanner
slides.body: One LLM call decomposes the goal into an ordered list of subtasks. A (often cheaper) Executor works through them one by one. A Replanner only gets invoked when a step fails or new information changes what's left to do.
bullets: Planner: single call, outputs a numbered plan like ['search X', 'extract Y', 'compile Z']
Executor: runs each step — a tool call or a delegated sub-agent — and returns the result
Replanner: compares progress against the remaining plan; continues, revises, or declares done
Traces back to Plan-and-Solve prompting and early agent frameworks like BabyAGI/LangChain's plan-and-execute agents

slides.title: Worked Example: Pricing Research Across 5 Companies
slides.body: Task: 'Compare pricing tiers for 5 competitor products and summarize the differences.'
bullets: Planner emits: 1) fetch pricing page for each of 5 companies 2) extract tiers 3) build comparison table 4) write summary
Steps 1-2 are independent per company, so the executor can dispatch them to parallel sub-agents instead of one sequential loop
Company C's pricing page requires login; only that one step fails — the Replanner swaps in a cached snippet instead of restarting the whole task
Total LLM 'thinking' calls: one plan + one replan, versus a ReAct trace that would re-reason at every single fetch and extraction

slides.title: ReAct vs. Plan-and-Execute

rows: Full plan upfront, revised on failure
One reasoning call per step, cost grows with trajectory length
One planning call, cheap execution, occasional replan calls
Hard — each step depends on the last turn's reasoning
Easy for independent steps once the plan is fixed
Exploratory tasks where the next step depends on what you just learned
Long tasks that decompose cleanly into a known structure

slides.title: When It Backfires
slides.body: A plan is a bet that the world won't change faster than you can react to it.
bullets: Bad fit for highly reactive tasks (live chat, fast-changing data) where re-planning overhead dominates any savings
A stale plan is worse than no plan: if step 2's result invalidates step 4 and nothing triggers a replan, later steps execute on wrong assumptions
Garbage in, garbage out — a vague goal produces a vague, unfollowable plan, and the executor has no way to fix that on its own
Debugging gets harder: a failure could be a bad decomposition (planner's fault) or a bad tool call (executor's fault), and telling them apart takes extra tracing

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Plan-and-Execute front-loads reasoning into one Planner call, so execution can be cheap, fast, and even parallel
Use it when a task decomposes cleanly; use ReAct when each step genuinely depends on unpredictable results from the last one
The split lets you pair an expensive frontier model for planning with a cheap, fast model for mechanical execution
Always wire in a Replanner path — a fixed plan with no revision mechanism turns one wrong assumption into total task failure

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of separating planning from execution?
options: It eliminates the need for any LLM calls
The planner reasons about the whole task once, so execution steps don't each need full-context re-reasoning
It guarantees the generated plan is always correct
It removes the need for tools entirely
questions.explanation: Plan-and-Execute front-loads the expensive 'what should happen' reasoning into a single planning call, letting execution be cheap and mostly mechanical — unless a step fails and the plan needs revising.

questions.prompt: In the ReAct pattern, what typically happens to cost as a task grows longer?
options: It stays constant since only the latest step is sent
It grows, because the full thought/action/observation trajectory is resent on every step
It decreases as the model 'learns' the pattern mid-task
It is unrelated to how many steps the task takes
questions.explanation: ReAct re-prompts with the accumulated trace at every turn, so cost and latency climb with step count — a key reason to plan ahead when a task is long and its structure is predictable.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer ReAct over Plan-and-Execute?
options: When the task is a long, fully predictable checklist
When you want to minimize the number of LLM calls
When each next step genuinely depends on unpredictable results from the previous action, like exploratory debugging
When steps need to run in parallel
questions.explanation: ReAct shines when you can't know step N+1 until you see the result of step N — adaptive, exploratory tasks. Plan-and-Execute shines when the task's structure is knowable upfront.

posts.title: Claude Code Makes Auto Mode the Default
posts.subtitle: Anthropic bets that a targeted classifier beats a human clicking 'approve' on reflex.
posts.summary: Starting August 14, 2026, Anthropic made 'auto mode' the default permission setting in Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Team plans, replacing per-action approval prompts with a classifier that only stops to ask about irreversible, destructive, or out-of-environment actions. The move follows internal testing showing human reviewers caught far fewer dangerous commands than the automated classifier did, on a backdrop of a 97% reflexive approval rate on the old prompt-every-time model.

slides.title: Claude Code Makes Auto Mode the Default
slides.body: As of August 14, 2026, new Claude Code sessions on Pro, Max, and Team plans no longer ask for approval before every tool call — auto mode is now the starting permission setting.

slides.title: 97% Approval Looks Like Trust — It's Actually Fatigue
bullets: Claude Code's old default asked for human approval before most tool calls (file edits, shell commands, etc.)
Anthropic reports about 97% of those permission prompts got approved
A rate that high across thousands of varied actions reads less like careful review and more like reflexive clicking

slides.title: A Classifier Replaces the Rubber Stamp
slides.body: In auto mode, Claude Code proceeds by default and only interrupts for actions a classifier judges irreversible, destructive, or aimed outside the working environment.
bullets: Rolling out first to Pro, Max, and Team plans; Enterprise, API, and cloud platform users follow within about a month per Anthropic's stated timeline
Users can still switch back to manual, per-action approval if they want the old behavior
The bar for interrupting is action-risk, not action-frequency — routine edits and reads no longer pause the agent

slides.title: The Test Behind the Switch
slides.body: Anthropic ran a purpose-built test environment with 1,053 paid testers to compare human review against the auto-mode classifier on the same dangerous commands.
bullets: Human reviewers, manually approving or blocking each action, caught the planted dangerous command in only about 13.6% of cases
The auto-mode classifier blocked the same class of dangerous commands roughly 89% of the time
The gap is the core justification: automated, risk-targeted checks outperformed people clicking through a wall of routine prompts

slides.title: Manual Approval vs. Auto Mode

rows: n/a — most actions proceed without asking

slides.title: What Auto Mode Doesn't Change
bullets: It's a default, not a lockout — manual approval mode is still available for users who want it
The classifier is imperfect: 89% blocked in testing means roughly 1 in 9 planted dangerous commands still got through
Rollout is plan-gated — Enterprise, API, and cloud-platform users were still on the old default at launch
It changes *when* Claude Code asks, not what counts as destructive — irreversible or out-of-environment actions still pause for a human

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Auto mode became the default for Claude Code on Pro, Max, and Team plans on August 14, 2026
The change is grounded in a specific finding: human approval on nearly every action produced a ~97% rubber-stamp rate and only ~13.6% dangerous-command detection
A risk-targeted classifier caught ~89% of the same dangerous commands in testing across 1,053 paid testers
It's a bet that fewer, better-targeted interruptions beat constant low-value ones — with the classifier's ~11% miss rate as the tradeoff

options: Enterprise and API customers only

posts.title: MCP Sampling: The Server Asks, the Client Decides
posts.subtitle: How a tool server borrows a real LLM completion without ever holding an API key.
posts.summary: Sampling is the MCP primitive that lets a server request an LLM completion through the connected client instead of holding its own model or API key. The client stays the trust boundary — it can review the outgoing prompt, pick the model, and inspect the completion before it ever reaches the server. That control comes at the cost of latency, optional support, and zero background autonomy for the server.

slides.title: MCP Sampling: The Server Asks, the Client Decides
slides.body: The third client-provided capability in MCP, alongside Roots and Elicitation, lets a server request a real LLM completion without ever touching an API key.

slides.title: Servers That Need Judgment Have No Model of Their Own
bullets: An MCP server exposes tools and resources to a host app (an IDE, a chat client) — it's plumbing, not a model
Some tasks still need judgment: 'summarize these 40 log lines,' 'pick the next browser action from this page state'
Hardcoding that logic is brittle; giving every server its own API key duplicates cost, credentials, and trust boundaries

slides.title: sampling/createMessage: One Request, Client-Owned
slides.body: A server sends a sampling/createMessage request over the existing MCP connection. The client, not the server, decides which model runs it and what comes back.
bullets: Request carries: messages, an optional systemPrompt, modelPreferences (cost/speed/intelligence hints from 0-1), maxTokens, temperature, stopSequences
includeContext scopes how much MCP context leaks into the prompt: 'none' | 'thisServer' | 'allServers'
The server gets back a completion only — never the client's API key or model choice

slides.title: The Round Trip Has a Human Checkpoint Built In
slides.body: Sampling is designed so a human can sit in the loop without the server knowing or caring.
bullets: 1) Server -> host client: sampling/createMessage request
2) Host can show the user the prompt for approval or edits before it goes anywhere
3) Host forwards the (possibly edited) prompt to its configured LLM and gets a completion
4) Host can show the user the completion before releasing it
5) Host -> server: the final completion, nothing else

slides.title: A Browser-Automation Server Delegates the Decision
slides.body: Concrete scenario: an MCP server drives a headless browser and doesn't ship its own vision-capable model.
bullets: Server captures the page state and sends a sampling request: 'given this DOM summary, what's the next click to finish checkout?'
The client's LLM — the same one the user is already talking to — reasons over it and replies 'click the button labeled Continue'
Server executes that answer through its own click tool: it borrowed reasoning, not raw model access

slides.title: Sampling vs. Roots vs. Elicitation

rows: Client tells the server which directories/URIs are in scope
Server asks the human directly for missing structured input

slides.title: Sampling Isn't Free, Instant, or Guaranteed
bullets: Optional capability: many hosts don't implement it, so servers need a fallback path when it's unsupported
Round-trip latency: a human-approval hop can turn a 'quick' decision into a multi-second wait, or longer
Cost sits with the client's subscription, not the server — a chatty server quietly burns the user's tokens
No background autonomy: a server can't sample unless the host app is open and connected

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: MCP servers don't need their own model or API key — they can ask the connected client to think for them
The client stays the trust boundary: it can inspect, edit, or reject both the outgoing prompt and the returned completion
Reach for it on in-tool judgment calls (next action, summarization, classification), not as a substitute for the host's own orchestration
It completes MCP's client-capability triad alongside Roots (scope) and Elicitation (ask the human directly)

questions.prompt: In MCP, which side actually runs the LLM when a server issues a sampling request?
options: The server, using its own API key
The client/host application, using its configured model
A dedicated MCP sampling service
Whichever side has lower latency
questions.explanation: Sampling is client-owned by design: the server sends a sampling/createMessage request, but the host application picks the model, can insert human review, and is the only side that ever touches an API key.

questions.prompt: What does includeContext control in a sampling request?
options: The temperature used for the completion
How much of the host's MCP context (this server's, or all connected servers') is included in the prompt
Which programming language the server is written in
The maximum token budget for the response
questions.explanation: includeContext ('none' | 'thisServer' | 'allServers') is a scoping control on how much surrounding MCP context leaks into the prompt sent to the model — it isn't a generation parameter like temperature or maxTokens.

questions.prompt: Why can't an MCP server rely on sampling for background, always-on autonomy?
options: Sampling requests are capped at 10 per day
Sampling only works with open-source models
The client/host must be connected and willing to forward the request, so nothing runs when the client isn't there
Sampling responses are always cached and never fresh
questions.explanation: Because the client owns the actual model call, a server has no path to a completion unless the host app is live and cooperating — sampling adds judgment to a connected session, it doesn't give the server independent runtime.

posts.title: ReAct: Reasoning and Acting in the Same Loop
posts.subtitle: The thought-action-observation pattern under nearly every modern tool-calling agent.
posts.summary: ReAct interleaves free-text reasoning with discrete tool actions and their observations in a single loop, letting a model both plan and correct course using real evidence instead of hallucinated facts. It's the pattern underneath today's tool-calling agent frameworks, but it isn't free — every step costs a full LLM call and errors can compound without backtracking.

slides.title: One Loop: Think, Act, Observe, Repeat
slides.body: ReAct (2022) interleaves reasoning traces with tool calls so a language model can plan, act in the world, and correct itself using what actually comes back.

slides.title: Reasoning Alone Can't Touch the World
slides.body: Chain-of-thought lets a model think step by step, but every 'fact' it uses comes from its own parameters — if it doesn't know something, it confidently makes it up.
bullets: Pure CoT: no way to fetch new information mid-answer, so knowledge gaps become hallucinations
Pure action-only agents (act without articulating a plan) can't explain their choices or notice an action failed until much later
Neither alone can both plan AND course-correct on live feedback

slides.title: Thought → Action → Observation, Repeat
slides.body: At each step the model emits a free-text Thought (what to do and why), then an Action (a discrete tool call like Search[query] or Lookup[term]), then receives an Observation (the tool's real output) appended to its context before the next Thought.
bullets: The full trajectory of prior thoughts/actions/observations conditions every next step
Loop continues until the model emits a Finish[answer] action
Needs only 1-2 in-context examples — no fine-tuning required in the original paper

slides.title: Worked Example: A Multi-Hop Question
slides.body: Q: 'What is the elevation range of the area the eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny extends into?' A pure CoT model might guess. ReAct instead grounds each hop in a real lookup.
bullets: Thought 1: I need to find what area the eastern sector of the Colorado orogeny extends into, so I'll search it
Action: Search[Colorado orogeny] → Observation: the orogeny's eastern sector extends into the High Plains
Thought 2: Now I need the elevation range of the High Plains → Action: Search[High Plains]
Observation gives the range → Thought 3: I have enough → Action: Finish[1,800 to 7,000 ft]

slides.title: The Numbers That Made It Stick
slides.body: Grounding in real tool output, not just reasoning, is what moved the needle on interactive tasks.

rows: Beats action-only; competitive with plain CoT

slides.title: Now It's the Default Agent Loop
slides.body: ReAct predates and underlies today's 'tool calling' or 'function calling' agent frameworks — OpenAI function calling, Claude tool use, LangChain/LangGraph agents all implement some version of this same Thought/Action/Observation cycle under different names.
bullets: Modern APIs formalize 'Action' as a structured tool-call schema instead of free-text like Search[query]
'Observation' is the tool result message appended back into the conversation
Multi-turn agent loops are, structurally, ReAct with better tooling

slides.title: Where It Breaks
slides.body: The loop has no native undo — it trusts its own trajectory.
bullets: Each step is a full extra LLM call: latency and cost scale linearly with iterations, unlike single-shot CoT
An early wrong Thought or a misread Observation compounds forward with no backtracking (later work like Reflexion adds self-critique to fix this)
Too few tools and the model can't act; too many and it starts calling the wrong one
On closed-book tasks where the model already knows the answer, plain CoT can actually beat ReAct — acting adds overhead with no new information to ground

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: ReAct = Thought (reason) → Action (tool call) → Observation (real feedback), looped until Finish
It wins specifically when the task needs external, verifiable information — not on pure reasoning problems
It's the ancestor of every modern tool-calling agent loop, just with structured schemas instead of free-text actions
Its weakness — no backtracking — is exactly what agent techniques like Reflexion were built to patch

questions.prompt: What three things does the ReAct loop interleave at each step?
options: Thought, Action, Observation
Plan, Execute, Reflect
Encode, Decode, Attend
Retrieve, Rank, Generate
questions.explanation: ReAct's loop is a free-text Thought (reasoning), a discrete Action (tool call), and an Observation (the tool's real result fed back into context) — repeated until the model emits a final answer.

questions.prompt: On which benchmarks did ReAct show its biggest gains over imitation/RL baselines, and why?
options: ALFWorld and WebShop, because acting in a real environment let it correct course on live feedback
MMLU and BBH, because they reward pure reasoning
GSM8K and MATH, because arithmetic benefits from tool calls
ImageNet and COCO, because vision tasks need grounding
questions.explanation: On the interactive ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, ReAct beat imitation/RL baselines by 34 and 10 absolute points respectively — the gain came from acting and observing real results, not from reasoning alone.

questions.prompt: What is a known failure mode of ReAct-style agents?
options: Early reasoning or tool-call errors compound forward because the loop has no built-in backtracking
They cannot be prompted with few-shot examples
They require full model fine-tuning before they work at all
They are unable to call more than one distinct tool across a whole task
questions.explanation: Because each step conditions on the entire prior trajectory, a wrong Thought or a misread Observation propagates forward with no native undo — techniques like Reflexion were later built specifically to add self-critique and recovery.

posts.title: BDH-CQ: Reasoning in Latent Space, No Chain of Thought
posts.subtitle: A 150M-parameter model beats the ARC-AGI-1 cost frontier by never writing down a thought.
posts.summary: Pathway's BDH-CQ solves ARC-AGI-style tasks by iterating a recurrent latent state instead of generating chain-of-thought text, reaching 29.5% pass@2 at $0.0007/task — a new cost-accuracy frontier, though independent replication is still pending.

slides.title: 150M Parameters, No Chain of Thought
bullets: Pathway's BDH-CQ reasons entirely inside a recurrent latent state — it never generates intermediate text.
On ARC-AGI-1 it hits 29.5% pass@2 at $0.0007 per task, breaking the benchmark's reported cost-accuracy frontier.

slides.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Is Expensive by Design
slides.body: Every token a reasoning model 'thinks out loud' costs compute and latency — a full forward pass per thought, even when the reasoning doesn't need to be language-shaped.
bullets: Frontier reasoning models spend thousands of output tokens per hard problem, each one billed and re-attended-over.
Pathway reports BDH-CQ running over 50x cheaper per task than larger transformer reasoners on ARC-AGI-style problems.

slides.title: Two Stages: Memorize, Then Compute
slides.body: BDH-CQ builds on Pathway's Dragon Hatchling (BDH) architecture: high-dimensional positive activations, low-rank communication, and a recurrent associative memory.
bullets: Stage 1 (memory acquisition): demonstrations are fed in sequentially; the recurrent state updates after each one, binding inputs to outputs.
Stage 2 (latent reasoning): the query is solved by iterating that same state in a high-dimensional latent workspace — no token is decoded until the final answer.
No chain-of-thought text is ever produced or attended over — that's where the cost savings come from.

slides.title: Cost-Accuracy Frontier
slides.body: These are Pathway's own reported numbers; independent reruns haven't landed yet.

rows: Larger transformer reasoners (e.g. GPT-5.6 Luna class)

slides.title: What a Demonstration Sequence Looks Like
slides.body: Feed the model a couple of ARC-AGI grid transformations (say, 'reflect and recolor'). Its recurrent state updates after each demo, without restating any of them — then a new grid arrives with no answer attached.
bullets: The model doesn't write 'I see the pattern is reflection...' — it iterates its latent state directly and decodes only the final grid.
Researchers ran controlled ARC-like interventions to probe which transformations it generalizes vs. merely memorizes.

slides.title: The Catch: No Interpretability, Narrow Domain
slides.body: Latent reasoning trades away the one thing chain-of-thought gives you for free: a human-readable trace of why the model answered the way it did.
bullets: You can't inspect why BDH-CQ reached an answer — there's no text trace to audit or debug.
Results so far are on ARC-AGI-style abstract-pattern tasks, not open-ended language reasoning.
These are Pathway's self-reported benchmarks; treat the headline cost numbers as promising, not settled, until independently replicated.

slides.title: Why This Matters
bullets: Test-time compute doesn't have to mean more output tokens — a recurrent latent state is a real alternative axis.
At 150M params, this runs on hardware a 70B+ reasoner never could.
Watch for independent replications before treating the cost numbers as final.

It uses a much larger context window
It fine-tunes its weights on each new task
It skips reasoning entirely and pattern-matches

By ingesting demonstrations sequentially into a recurrent memory that updates after each one
By retrieving similar tasks from a vector database
By generating and grading its own chain-of-thought

questions.explanation: Because reasoning never surfaces as text, you lose the auditable step-by-step trace chain-of-thought models give you for free.

posts.title: GLM-5.3: Same Base Model, Big Coding and Cyber Jump
posts.subtitle: Z.ai squeezed a 6x jump on Terminal-Bench out of post-training alone — then delayed the weights.
posts.summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.3, released August 14, 2026, reuses GLM-5.2's base model but posts large post-training-only gains on long-horizon coding and vulnerability-discovery benchmarks — capable enough that Z.ai is delaying open weights for a safety review.

slides.title: Post-Training Alone, Not a New Pretrain
bullets: Z.ai released GLM-5.3 on August 14, 2026, built on the exact same mixture-of-experts base as GLM-5.2.
Every benchmark gain reported comes from extended post-training — no new foundation model underneath.

slides.title: Why Reuse the Base Model?
slides.body: Pretraining a new foundation model costs enormous compute. Z.ai's bet: GLM-5.2's base still had headroom to extract through better post-training alone.
bullets: Terminal-Bench 3.0 moved from 4.6 to 28.3 — roughly a 6x jump — from post-training changes only.
DeepSWE v1.1 moved from 46.2 to 66.9; ExploitBench moved from 24.4% to 54.4%.

slides.title: Where the Gains Concentrate
slides.body: The jump is sharpest on the longest-horizon, most agentic tasks — ones requiring sustained multi-step tool use, not single-shot completions.
bullets: Terminal-Bench 3.0 (long-horizon terminal agent tasks) shows the single biggest jump of any benchmark Z.ai reported.
CyberGym (vulnerability discovery) reached 84.5%, edging past Claude Mythos 5 (83.8%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (83.6%) per Z.ai's own numbers.

slides.title: The Cybersecurity Surprise
slides.body: During evaluation, GLM-5.3 surfaced 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 open-source projects — 1,097 rated critical or high severity.
bullets: That capability jump is why Z.ai calls this its first explicitly cybersecurity-motivated weight delay.
Open weights and full API access are held back roughly two weeks past the August 14 release for safety hardening.

slides.title: What's Actually Available Right Now
slides.body: GLM-5.3 ships day-one only through Z.ai's own GLM Coding Plan and ZCode — not as open weights, breaking the pattern GLM-5.2 set.
bullets: GLM-5.2 shipped MIT-licensed weights within days of release; GLM-5.3 does not.
No per-token API pricing has been published yet — only Coding Plan subscription tiers (roughly $18 / $72 / $160 per month).
Every benchmark number above is Z.ai's own report on its own benchmark mix — not yet independently verified.

slides.title: Why It Matters
bullets: Post-training-only jumps this large suggest base models still have a lot of unclaimed capability left on the table.
A frontier open-weight lab voluntarily delaying weights for offensive-cyber capability is a new precedent, not routine caution.
Watch for the delayed weight/API release in ~2 weeks and for independent benchmark reruns before trusting the numbers fully.

posts.title: Mamba: Sequence Modeling Without Quadratic Attention
posts.subtitle: A selective state space that scans in linear time and still remembers what matters.
posts.summary: Mamba replaces self-attention's all-pairs comparison with a selective state space model: a recurrent state whose update rule is a function of the current token, giving linear-time compute and fixed-size memory — at the cost of exact long-range retrieval.

slides.title: Attention's O(n²) Problem, Solved Differently
bullets: Self-attention compares every token to every other token — cost grows quadratically with sequence length.
Mamba replaces that with a selective state space model (SSM): a recurrent state updated in linear time per token.

slides.title: Why Quadratic Attention Doesn't Scale
slides.body: Doubling context length quadruples attention's compute and memory. At very long contexts, the KV cache and attention matrix dominate cost long before parameter count does.
bullets: A 128K-token context needs roughly 16x the attention compute of an 8K context, for the same model.
Earlier linear-time alternatives (vanilla RNNs, linear attention) traded that cost away but lost selectivity — everything decays at the same fixed rate regardless of content.

slides.title: Selective State Spaces: Let the Input Choose the Decay
slides.body: Classic SSMs (S4) use fixed, input-independent transition matrices — efficient but unable to decide what to keep. Mamba makes the SSM's parameters (Δ, B, C) functions of the current input token.
bullets: Each token can write itself hard into the state, decay quickly, or pass through unchanged — recovering the content-based selectivity attention gets from softmax, without materializing an O(n²) matrix.
The recurrence is computed with a hardware-aware parallel scan, not step-by-step, so it still trains fast on GPUs despite being 'recurrent.'

slides.title: Attention vs. Selective State Space
slides.body: The headline win is inference: a fixed-size recurrent state means memory doesn't grow with context length the way a KV cache does.

slides.title: A Concrete Walkthrough
slides.body: Processing a 100K-token document: a Transformer keeps a KV cache entry for every one of those tokens, growing linearly and attended over quadratically each step.
bullets: Mamba keeps one fixed-size hidden state updated per token — the 100,001st token costs the same to process as the 2nd.
This is why Mamba-based and hybrid models get cited for cheap long-context inference rather than for raw benchmark accuracy alone.

slides.title: Where Mamba Falls Short
slides.body: Selectivity fixes the 'forget everything' problem, but a fixed-size state is still a bottleneck compared to attention's full lookback.
bullets: Tasks needing exact retrieval of one specific fact from far back in a long context (needle-in-a-haystack) tend to favor attention — Mamba must compress everything through its state.

Pure-SSM models have generally underperformed similarly-sized Transformers on some in-context-learning and copying benchmarks, which is why many production models hybridize Mamba layers with a few attention layers instead of going pure-SSM.
Don't reach for Mamba just for 'efficiency' on short, retrieval-heavy tasks — the win shows up at long sequence lengths.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Mamba trades attention's full pairwise comparison for a selective, input-dependent recurrent state — linear time, fixed memory.
The 'selective' part is the key idea: it recovers content-based reasoning that older RNNs and linear attention couldn't do.
Best used for long-context or streaming workloads, or hybridized with attention layers — not as a universal drop-in replacement.

questions.prompt: What's the core difference between Mamba's SSM and a classic (S4) state space model?
options: Mamba uses a much larger hidden state
Mamba's transition parameters (Δ, B, C) are functions of the input token, making the state update selective
Mamba removes the recurrent state entirely
Mamba only works on text, not other sequence types
questions.explanation: S4's transition matrices are fixed regardless of input; Mamba makes them input-dependent, so the model can choose what to remember or forget per token — that's the 'selective' in selective state space model.

questions.prompt: Why does Mamba's inference memory stay roughly constant as context length grows, unlike a Transformer's?
options: It uses quantization to compress the KV cache
It maintains one fixed-size recurrent state instead of a cache that grows with every token
It truncates old tokens after a fixed window
It runs on specialized hardware with more memory
questions.explanation: A Transformer's KV cache stores an entry per past token, growing linearly; Mamba compresses everything seen so far into one fixed-size state vector, so memory doesn't scale with sequence length.

questions.prompt: When should you be cautious about choosing a pure Mamba model over a Transformer?
options: When you need long-context efficiency
When the task requires exact retrieval of one specific fact from far back in a long context
When you want linear time complexity
When compute budget is limited
questions.explanation: Because Mamba compresses history into a fixed-size state, exact needle-in-haystack retrieval is harder than for attention, which can look back at every token directly — this is why many production systems hybridize Mamba with a few attention layers.
