posts.title: Bloom Filters: Checking Membership Without the Set
posts.subtitle: A structure that answers 'maybe' or 'definitely not' — and never 'yes' for certain
posts.summary: A Bloom filter is a fixed-size bit array plus a handful of hash functions that lets you test set membership in O(k) time using a fraction of the memory a hash set needs. It never produces a false negative, but it can produce false positives — which is exactly the tradeoff that makes it useful as a cheap pre-filter in front of an expensive lookup.

slides.title: Answer 'have I seen this before?' without storing what you've seen
slides.body: Bloom filters trade a small, tunable false-positive rate for a massive reduction in memory versus storing every key.

slides.title: A hash set doesn't scale to billions of keys
slides.body: Checking 'is this URL malicious?' or 'does this key already exist?' against millions or billions of items with a real hash set means storing every key (or its hash) plus per-entry overhead — tens of gigabytes at scale, and most of that memory is spent on entries you'll never actually need to retrieve.
bullets: A hash set entry typically costs 40-100+ bytes once you include object overhead and load-factor headroom
At 1 billion keys that's 40-100+ GB just to answer yes/no questions
You often don't need the key back — you only need to know if it's probably there

slides.title: The mechanism: a bit array and k hash functions
slides.body: A Bloom filter is an array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions.
bullets: Insert(x): compute k hashes of x, set those k bit positions to 1
Query(x): compute the same k hashes; if ALL k bits are 1 → 'maybe present'; if ANY bit is 0 → 'definitely absent'
No false negatives are possible: if x was inserted, all its bits are guaranteed set
False positives are possible: another combination of inserted items can happen to set all of x's bits even though x was never inserted

slides.title: Worked example: a tiny 16-bit filter
slides.body: m = 16 bits, k = 2 hash functions. Insert 'cat' → sets bits 3 and 9. Insert 'dog' → sets bits 5 and 9.
bullets: Query 'cat': bits 3 and 9 are both 1 → correctly reports 'maybe present'
Query 'fish': happens to hash to bits 3 and 5 — both already set by 'cat' and 'dog' → reports 'maybe present' even though 'fish' was never inserted (a false positive)
Query 'bird': hashes to bit 12, which is 0 → correctly reports 'definitely absent', no disk or database lookup needed
Real system example: Cassandra checks a Bloom filter per SSTable before touching disk, skipping reads for keys that definitely aren't in that file

slides.title: Bloom filter vs. hash set
Sizing it: the formulas that matter
slides.body: The false-positive rate depends on bit-array size m, number of hashes k, and number of inserted elements n: p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. The optimal number of hash functions is k = (m/n) · ln(2).
bullets: To hit a 1% target false-positive rate, you need roughly 9.6 bits per element and about 7 hash functions
Undersizing m for the actual n is the most common real-world mistake — as the filter fills up, the false-positive rate climbs sharply, not linearly
Because m must be fixed upfront, you need a reasonable estimate of n before deploying

slides.title: When not to reach for one
slides.body: A Bloom filter is a pre-filter, not a source of truth — treat it as an optimization, not the final answer.
bullets: You can't delete an item without a counting Bloom filter (extra memory per slot to track reference counts)
You can't list what's actually in the set — only test individual membership
A 'maybe present' answer still requires a real lookup to confirm — it only saves you the lookups for items that are 'definitely absent'
If your expected element count is unknown or highly variable, a fixed-size filter will either waste memory or blow past its target false-positive rate

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Bloom filters trade a small, tunable false-positive rate for large memory savings versus a hash set
They never produce false negatives — 'definitely absent' can be trusted outright, skipping an expensive lookup
'Maybe present' still needs a real check — the filter is a cheap gate in front of expensive work, not a replacement for it
Size m and k for your expected n up front: ~9.6 bits/element and k≈7 gets you a 1% false-positive rate

questions.prompt: If a Bloom filter query returns 'definitely absent' for an item, what can you conclude?
options: The item might still be in the set
The item is guaranteed not to be in the set
The filter is misconfigured
You need to run the query again with different hash functions
questions.explanation: Bloom filters never produce false negatives. If any of the item's k bits is 0, it's mathematically guaranteed that item was never inserted — you can skip the expensive lookup entirely.

questions.prompt: Why can a Bloom filter report a false positive?
options: Because hash functions occasionally return wrong values
Because bits set by other inserted items can coincidentally cover all of a queried item's positions, even though it was never inserted
Because the bit array resets randomly
Because k is always set to 1
questions.explanation: Multiple items share the same bit array. If enough other insertions happen to set exactly the bits a never-inserted item would hash to, the filter can't tell the difference — it reports 'maybe present' when the true answer is 'no.'

questions.prompt: What's a real limitation that should stop you from using a plain Bloom filter?
options: Needing to delete individual items from the set later
Needing to check if an item exists quickly
Having a rough upfront estimate of how many elements you'll store
Wanting to reduce memory versus a hash set
questions.explanation: A standard Bloom filter has no delete operation — clearing a bit could break lookups for other items that also hash to it. Deletion requires a counting Bloom filter variant with extra per-slot memory.

posts.title: Tokenization: The Boundary Between Text and the Model
posts.subtitle: One merge-the-most-frequent-pair algorithm decides how text becomes tokens — and that quietly sets your cost, your context budget, and why the model can't count letters.
posts.summary: Byte-pair encoding builds a subword vocabulary bottom-up: start from raw bytes, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair, and stop once you hit a target vocab size — that's how every modern LLM turns text into the token IDs it actually processes. The vocab-size choice is a real tradeoff between sequence length and embedding-table size, and it explains three practical realities: why token costs vary by language, why models struggle to count letters inside words, and why swapping a tokenizer means retraining the embedding table from scratch.

slides.title: Tokenization: The Boundary Between Text and the Model
slides.body: Before a single weight multiplies anything, raw text has to become a sequence of integers. The algorithm that does that — byte-pair encoding — quietly shapes cost, context budget, and even which languages a model is good at.

slides.title: Why Not Just Use Characters or Words?
slides.body: Both extremes fail for practical LLMs.
bullets: Character-level vocab is tiny (~256 bytes) but turns every sentence into a very long sequence — and attention cost grows with sequence length, so long character sequences are expensive to process
Word-level vocab keeps sequences short but is unbounded: new words, typos, and rare compounds constantly appear, forcing an <unk> token for anything unseen during training
Neither extreme handles the boundary between languages, code identifiers, or made-up words gracefully — subword tokenization is the compromise that ships in every modern LLM

slides.title: Byte-Pair Encoding: Merge the Most Frequent Pair, Repeat
slides.body: BPE started as a 1994 compression algorithm; Sennrich et al. adapted it for NLP subword vocabularies in 2015, and GPT-2 made byte-level BPE the modern default.
bullets: Start with a base vocabulary of individual bytes/characters — every possible input is representable from the start, so there's no <unk> token
Scan the training corpus, count how often every adjacent pair of symbols co-occurs, and merge the single most frequent pair into one new symbol
Repeat: each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary and shortens the corpus, stopping once the vocab hits its target size — a hyperparameter chosen before training, e.g. 50k or 100k
Encoding new text re-applies the learned merges in the order they were discovered — common words collapse to one token, rare or unseen words fall back to smaller, more numerous pieces

slides.title: A Toy Merge, Step by Step
slides.body: Run BPE on a tiny corpus of {low, lower, lowest, newer, wider} (each split into characters plus an end-of-word marker), and the first few merges look like this:
bullets: Pair 'e'+'r' is the most frequent adjacent pair (it appears in lower, newer, wider) → merge into a new symbol 'er'
Next most frequent: 'er'+ end-of-word → merge into 'er</w>', so 'newer' and 'wider' now end in one token instead of two
Next: 'l'+'o' → 'lo', then 'lo'+'w' → 'low' — 'low', 'lower', and 'lowest' now all start from the shared token 'low' instead of four separate letters
After a handful of merges, frequent words compress to 1-2 tokens while rare strings stay as longer chains of smaller pieces — exactly the tradeoff a real tokenizer makes at scale

slides.title: Vocab Size Is a Real Design Choice, Not a Detail
slides.body: Bigger vocab means fewer tokens per sentence (shorter sequences, more text fits in a fixed context window) but a bigger embedding and output-projection matrix, and more rarely-seen tokens that get little gradient signal during training.

slides.title: The Same Sentence Isn't the Same Number of Tokens
slides.body: Tokenizers are trained on corpora dominated by English web text, so the compression they learn is lopsided.
bullets: OpenAI's own rule of thumb for English: roughly 4 characters, or about 0.75 words, per token — so 75 English words costs around 100 tokens
The same sentence translated into a script the tokenizer saw far less of during training (Hindi, Burmese, Amharic, etc.) can take several times as many tokens to encode the identical meaning

Since API pricing and context-window limits are both counted in tokens, that inflation directly means higher cost and less usable context for speakers of underrepresented languages — a measurable effect, not a hypothetical one
The fix isn't free either: a wider, more multilingual vocabulary costs more embedding parameters and dilutes how often any single token is seen during training

slides.title: Where Tokenization Bites You
slides.body: Most 'why did the model get this obviously simple thing wrong' moments trace back to tokenization, not reasoning.
bullets: Letter-counting and spelling tasks ('how many r's in strawberry') are hard because the model never sees individual letters — it sees whatever subword pieces the tokenizer happened to split the word into

Multi-digit arithmetic used to be unreliable partly because digits didn't tokenize consistently — numbers like '380' and '381' could split at different boundaries, breaking the positional pattern the model needed to learn

Rare vocabulary entries that exist in the trained vocab but almost never appear in the training data can produce erratic output when prompted directly — a known failure mode sometimes called a 'glitch token'

Fine-tuning a base model onto a domain its tokenizer rarely saw (a new programming language, heavy code-switching, dense math notation) inflates token counts and degrades quality — swapping tokenizers means retraining the embedding table from scratch

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: BPE builds a vocabulary bottom-up: start from bytes/characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair, stop at a target vocab size
Byte-level BPE (GPT-2 onward) guarantees every input is representable — there's no out-of-vocabulary token, just longer chains of smaller pieces
Vocab size is a real tradeoff: a bigger vocab means shorter sequences and more usable context per token budget, at the cost of a larger embedding table and more undertrained rare tokens
Pricing, context limits, and even letter-counting ability are all downstream of how text gets chopped into tokens — tokenization isn't plumbing you can ignore, it's a first-order design choice

questions.prompt: What problem does byte-level BPE solve that plain word-level tokenization can't?
options: It makes the vocabulary smaller than character-level tokenization
It guarantees every possible input string is representable, eliminating the need for an <unk> token
It removes the need for an embedding table entirely
It ensures every word maps to exactly one token regardless of language
questions.explanation: Word-level vocabularies are unbounded — new words, typos, and rare compounds constantly appear, forcing an <unk> token for anything unseen. Because byte-level BPE's base vocabulary is every possible byte, any input string can always be represented, worst case as a long chain of single-byte tokens.

questions.prompt: In the toy BPE walkthrough, why does 'e'+'r' get merged before 'l'+'o'?
options: 'er' appears alphabetically first
BPE always merges vowel-consonant pairs first
'e'+'r' is the most frequent adjacent pair in the training corpus at that step
'er' is a complete English word, so it's prioritized
questions.explanation: BPE has no notion of grammar or alphabetization — at every step it counts adjacent-pair frequency across the whole training corpus and merges whichever pair occurs most often. 'e'+'r' shows up in 'lower', 'newer', and 'wider', making it the top count in that toy corpus.

questions.prompt: Why can the same sentence cost noticeably more tokens in one language than another, using the same tokenizer?
options: Some languages have more letters in their alphabet
The tokenizer was trained on a corpus dominated by one language/script, so it learned fewer efficient merges for underrepresented scripts
Non-English text is always converted to English before tokenization
Tokenizers assign a fixed token budget per language
questions.explanation: BPE's merges are learned from training-corpus frequency. A tokenizer trained mostly on English web text spends most of its merge budget on English subwords, so a script it saw far less of falls back to longer chains of smaller pieces for the same meaning — directly increasing token count, cost, and effective context usage for that language.

posts.title: Write-Ahead Logging: Surviving a Crash Mid-Write
posts.subtitle: One rule — write the log record before the data page — is what lets a database recover a torn write instead of losing it.
posts.summary: Write-ahead logging enforces one invariant: a log record describing a change must be durable on disk before the data page it describes is allowed to be. That single rule turns crash recovery from guesswork into a deterministic replay, and it's why Postgres, MySQL's InnoDB, SQLite, and most production databases are all built around a WAL rather than writing data pages in place and hoping.

slides.title: Write-Ahead Logging: Surviving a Crash Mid-Write
slides.body: Update a data page in place, crash halfway through the write, and you're left with a torn page — half old bytes, half new, and no way to tell which. WAL exists to make that scenario recoverable.

slides.title: In-Place Writes Have No Way Back
slides.body: Disk pages are usually several kilobytes; a power loss or crash can interrupt a write partway through, and a naive in-place update leaves no record of what the page looked like before.
bullets: A torn page mixes bytes from the old and new versions — the page is neither the pre-transaction nor post-transaction state, just corrupt
Fsyncing every data page write for safety is slow: data pages are scattered across the disk, so durable writes mean random I/O
Without a separate record of intent, recovery after a crash has nothing to replay or roll back — the on-disk state is just whatever the crash left behind

slides.title: The WAL Invariant
slides.body: Write-ahead logging enforces one rule, and everything else follows from it.
bullets: Rule: the log record describing a change must be flushed to durable storage before the data page it describes is allowed to be flushed
The log is append-only — writes are always sequential, so a single fsync can durably commit many log records at once instead of one random write per page

Because the log is the durable source of truth, the actual data pages can be updated in memory and flushed to disk lazily, whenever it's convenient (a 'steal, no-force' buffer policy) — the log guarantees nothing is lost if a crash happens before that lazy flush

slides.title: LSNs Tie Every Page Back to the Log
slides.body: ARIES (Mohan et al., 1992), the recovery algorithm most production databases descend from, ties pages to the log with a single number.
bullets: Every log record gets a monotonically increasing Log Sequence Number (LSN) marking its position in the log
Every data page stores the LSN of the last log record that modified it (its pageLSN)
On recovery, comparing a page's pageLSN to the log tells you exactly which log records still need to be replayed onto that page — no guessing
Checkpoints periodically record the oldest LSN that might still need replaying, so recovery doesn't have to scan the entire log history back to the beginning of time

slides.title: Recovery: In-Place Writes vs. WAL

rows: Log record is either fully durable or not written at all; page state is always reconstructable
Random I/O — fsync scattered across data pages
Sequential append to the log — one fsync can durably cover many changes
None — no record of prior state to replay
Deterministic: redo committed changes from the log, undo uncommitted ones
Must be synchronous to be safe
Can be lazy/asynchronous — the log already guarantees durability

slides.title: A Transaction, Two Crash Points
slides.body: Same transaction — transfer $50 — crashing at two different moments shows what the log rule actually buys you.
bullets: Transaction writes a log record ('debit account A $50, credit account B $50') and calls fsync on the log, then updates the in-memory data pages
Crash AFTER the log fsync but BEFORE the data pages are flushed: on restart, recovery reads the durable log record and redoes the update — no data lost
Crash BEFORE the log fsync completes: the log record never became durable, so on restart there's nothing to redo — the transaction simply never happened, and account balances stay consistent
The one crash point WAL rules out entirely: log record durable, but the transaction only half-applied with no way to know what's missing — that's exactly the invariant it enforces

slides.title: What WAL Doesn't Solve
slides.body: WAL protects physical consistency across a crash — it isn't a general-purpose safety net.
bullets: An unbounded WAL fills the disk — it must be checkpointed and archived/recycled once its records are no longer needed for recovery or replication
Checkpointing itself briefly increases write latency, since dirty pages up to the checkpoint LSN must be flushed
WAL doesn't protect against logical errors — an UPDATE with the wrong WHERE clause gets faithfully logged and replayed too

If the log storage itself is corrupted or the fsync guarantee is broken (e.g. a disk write cache lying about durability), the entire recovery guarantee collapses — WAL is only as durable as the fsync beneath it

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The core invariant is simple: log the change durably before the data page it describes is allowed to be durable
Sequential log writes turn expensive random-I/O durability into cheap append-only durability, letting data pages flush lazily
LSNs on both log records and data pages are what make recovery deterministic instead of a guessing game — ARIES's analysis/redo/undo phases are built entirely on comparing them
WAL guarantees physical crash consistency, not correctness — it will faithfully replay a logically wrong write just as reliably as a correct one

questions.prompt: What is the core invariant that write-ahead logging enforces?
options: Data pages must be written before their corresponding log record
The log record describing a change must be durable on disk before the data page it describes is allowed to be durable
Every write must be synchronous and fsynced individually, whether logged or not
Log records and data pages must always be written to the same physical disk sector
questions.explanation: The name says it: write-AHEAD logging means the log entry hits durable storage first. That ordering is what makes a crash recoverable — the log always has an accurate record of what should have happened, even if the data page update never made it to disk.

questions.prompt: Why does WAL improve write throughput compared to fsyncing every data page update in place?
options: It eliminates the need for durability entirely, since data pages are treated as disposable
It skips writing to disk and keeps everything in memory permanently
The log is append-only and sequential, so many changes can be made durable with a single sequential fsync, while data pages flush lazily and asynchronously afterward
It compresses data pages before writing them, reducing I/O volume
questions.explanation: Data pages are scattered across disk, so fsyncing each one is random I/O. The log is append-only, so a single sequential fsync can durably commit a batch of log records at once — and because the log already guarantees durability, the actual data pages can be flushed later, in memory-efficient batches, without any durability risk.

questions.prompt: In ARIES-style recovery, what is a pageLSN used for?
options: It encrypts the page contents for security
It records the LSN of the last log record that modified that page, letting recovery know exactly which log records still need to be replayed onto it
It tracks which user session most recently read the page
It sets an expiration time after which the page is automatically deleted
questions.explanation: Comparing a page's stored pageLSN against the log tells recovery precisely which updates are already reflected on that page and which still need to be redone — eliminating any guesswork about what state the page was left in when the crash happened.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Only Some Weights Fire Per Token
posts.subtitle: How trillion-parameter models keep inference cheap by routing each token to a handful of specialists.
posts.summary: Dense transformers spend every parameter on every token, so bigger models cost proportionally more to run. Mixture of Experts splits the feed-forward layer into many smaller experts and routes each token to only a handful of them, decoupling total capacity from per-token compute — the trick behind models like Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 that pack hundreds of billions of parameters while activating a fraction per forward pass.

slides.title: The Trick Behind Models That Don't Cost as Much as They Weigh
slides.body: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is the architecture inside Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, and most of today's largest open models: swap the single dense feed-forward layer for many smaller expert networks, and route each token to only a few of them.

slides.title: Dense Transformers Charge Full Price for Every Token
bullets: Every token passes through every parameter in a dense feed-forward layer, so FLOPs-per-token scale directly with total parameter count.
Going from a 7B to a 70B dense model doesn't just add capacity — it multiplies inference cost roughly 10x for every single token, even trivial ones like punctuation.
Scaling laws reward bigger models, but dense scaling means training and serving cost grow in lockstep with quality — there's no way to add capacity without paying for it on every forward pass.

slides.title: Split the Feed-Forward Layer, Then Route Instead of Compute
bullets: Replace the single dense feed-forward block in a transformer layer with N smaller feed-forward networks ('experts') plus a lightweight router — a small learned linear layer.
For each token, the router scores all N experts and picks the top-k (commonly k=2): only those experts run their FFN on that token, and the rest sit idle for it.
The token's output is a weighted sum of the chosen experts' outputs, weighted by the router's own scores — the router trains end to end with the rest of the model, no separate objective needed.

slides.title: An Unconstrained Router Collapses Onto a Few Favorites
bullets: Left unconstrained, the router tends to concentrate traffic on whichever experts get an early lead in training, starving the rest of gradient signal — the opposite of the specialization the design is after.
The standard fix is an auxiliary load-balancing loss added to the training objective, penalizing uneven routing and pushing usage back toward uniform across experts.

Production systems also cap each expert's 'capacity' — the max tokens it will accept per batch. Tokens that overflow a full expert get dropped or rerouted, which makes capacity factor a real serving-time tuning knob, not just a training detail.

slides.title: Dense vs. Mixture of Experts
bullets: The headline win is compute, not memory — an MoE model still needs enough VRAM to hold every expert, even though most sit idle on any given token.

rows: Scales with active parameters only (top-k experts)
A dense 70B model: ~70B params active on every token
Mixtral 8x7B: 47B total params, ~13B active per token (2 of 8 experts)
= total parameters — every expert must stay resident
Expert parallelism, all-to-all token routing across devices

slides.title: DeepSeek-V3: 671B Total Parameters, ~37B Active
bullets: DeepSeek-V3 uses a fine-grained MoE design: 256 routed experts plus a shared expert per layer, with each token activating 8 of the 256 routed experts — about 3% of the routed pool.
Total parameter count is 671B, but only around 37B are active for any single token's forward pass — roughly the compute cost of a dense 37B model, with far more total specialized capacity to draw on.

That gap is the entire point: quality tracks total parameters (more specialized capacity to route into), while latency and FLOPs track active parameters (what actually runs) — MoE decouples two numbers a dense model forces to be equal.

slides.title: Where MoE Stops Paying Off
bullets: Memory doesn't shrink — serving a large MoE still requires GPU memory (or multi-GPU sharding) for the full parameter count, so small-scale or single-GPU deployments often see no benefit over a smaller dense model with similar active compute.

All-to-all communication between devices — sending each token to whichever GPU holds its chosen expert — becomes the bottleneck at scale; large MoE systems are usually communication-bound, not FLOPs-bound, once sharded across a cluster.
Fine-tuning is trickier: a small fine-tuning dataset can retrain the router into a degenerate few-expert pattern, quietly discarding most of the model's specialized capacity.

At small batch sizes, the router adds a step with no payoff — there aren't enough concurrent tokens to keep multiple experts busy in parallel, so a dense model of similar active size can be simpler and just as fast.

slides.title: When to Reach for This
bullets: MoE trades total-parameter growth for active-parameter cost — more capacity without a proportional compute bill, as long as you can afford to keep every expert resident in memory.
The router and load-balancing loss aren't optional extras — an unconstrained router collapses onto a few experts and quietly throws away most of the model's capacity.

Reach for MoE when serving at scale with enough batch size and multi-GPU/multi-node infrastructure to amortize communication cost; skip it for single-GPU, latency-critical, or low-traffic deployments where a dense model is simpler and just as fast.

questions.prompt: In a Mixture-of-Experts layer with top-2 routing over 8 experts, how many experts actually run their feed-forward network for a given token?
options: All 8
It depends on the token's length
questions.explanation: Top-k routing with k=2 means the router selects the 2 highest-scoring experts for that token, and only those two run their FFN — the other 6 sit idle for it, which is exactly where MoE's compute savings come from.

questions.prompt: Why does an MoE model still need GPU memory for its full parameter count, even though it activates only a fraction per token?
options: Because the router itself is enormous
Because every expert must stay resident in memory since any token could route to any of them
Because MoE models don't actually save any compute
Because gradients require double the memory
questions.explanation: Which experts a given token needs isn't known until the router scores it at inference time, so every expert has to already be loaded and ready — MoE saves compute per token, not memory footprint.

questions.prompt: What does the auxiliary load-balancing loss in MoE training prevent?
options: The model from training at all
The router from collapsing onto a small subset of favorite experts
Tokens from being processed in parallel
The need for a router altogether
questions.explanation: Without a balancing signal, the router tends to concentrate traffic on whichever experts get an early lead, starving the rest of gradient updates — the auxiliary loss pushes usage back toward uniform so the model actually uses its full expert capacity.

posts.title: Orchard: Training Agents Inside Their Real Deployment Tools
posts.subtitle: No more train-in-a-toy-box, deploy-in-the-real-world gap.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's Orchard is an open-source, Kubernetes-native framework that trains agents directly inside the same harnesses (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw) they'll be deployed in. Its three recipes hit 69.7% (73% with reranking) on SWE-bench Verified, 68.4% average across three GUI-navigation benchmarks, and 73.9% on a personal-assistant eval — while spinning up 1,000 sandboxes in 26 seconds.

slides.title: Train the Agent Where It Will Actually Live
slides.body: Orchard, published by Microsoft Research on August 3, 2026, is an open-source framework for training agents directly inside their real deployment harnesses instead of a separate simulator.

slides.title: Most Agent Training Happens in the Wrong Environment
bullets: Coding and GUI agents are usually trained in a simplified sandbox, then shipped into a real harness like Codex, OpenClaw, or ZeroClaw for actual use.
Every mismatch between the training environment and the deployment harness — tool names, prompt formats, error strings — is a place the agent's learned policy can silently break.
Standing up thousands of isolated, reproducible environments for RL at scale is itself an infrastructure problem most research groups don't want to own.

slides.title: One Kubernetes-Native Layer, Three Domain Recipes
bullets: Orchard Env is a lightweight Kubernetes-native sandbox service: a REST API plus Python SDK that spins up isolated containers on demand, with an average 0.28s command-execution latency.
It launched 1,000 sandboxes in parallel in 26 seconds in Microsoft's own benchmarking, and works with any base image plus preinstalled harnesses like Codex, Claude, OpenClaw, and ZeroClaw.
On top sits a Trainer — an RL stack built on a vendored fork of the slime training framework — and three domain-specific 'recipes': Orchard-SWE, Orchard-GUI, and Orchard-Claw.

slides.title: Three Recipes, Three Real Scores
bullets: The GUI agent is small — 4B parameters — and trained on only 400 demonstrations plus 2,200 RL tasks, yet still clears 74% on WebVoyager.
Orchard-Claw's score nearly triples (59.6% → 73.9%) once it's paired with the ZeroClaw deployment system — the harness itself is part of the result, not just the model.

slides.title: Orchard-SWE, Walked Through
bullets: The team distilled 107,000 interaction trajectories from larger teacher models (MiniMax-M2.5 and Qwen3.5-397B) into a much smaller ~3B-active-parameter Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts model.
Training happened inside the Mini-SWE-Agent harness — the same kind of tool-calling loop the model sees in production — not a custom training-only simulator.
Result: 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified (73% once a value-model reranks candidate patches), with 51.0% on a multilingual variant and 45.0% when evaluated under a harness it wasn't trained in.

slides.title: The Gap That Doesn't Close: New Harness, New Drop
bullets: Training inside the deployment harness narrows the train/deploy gap for that specific harness — but Orchard-SWE still loses roughly 24 points (69.7% → 45%) when tested under an unseen harness.
Kubernetes-native infrastructure is the whole point, but it's also the cost: this isn't a laptop-friendly framework, it assumes cluster access most solo researchers don't have.
Reranking adds real inference-time cost (an extra value-model pass per candidate) for that jump from 69.7% to 73%, a tradeoff worth knowing before assuming the headline number is free.

slides.title: Why This Matters for Anyone Building Agents
bullets: Matching the training environment to the deployment harness is treated as a first-class design decision, not an afterthought — and the numbers show it isn't free once the harness changes.
A small, MoE-style model (~3B active params) getting to 69.7% on SWE-bench Verified is a reminder that infrastructure and data quality can matter as much as raw parameter count.
Open-sourcing Orchard Env, the recipes, and a 107K-trajectory dataset on Hugging Face lowers the bar for other labs to reproduce or extend this instead of rebuilding sandbox infra from scratch.

questions.prompt: What is Orchard's core design idea for closing the agent train/deploy gap?
options: Train in a faster, simplified simulator and fine-tune after deployment
Train the agent directly inside the same harness (Codex, OpenClaw, ZeroClaw) it will be deployed in
Skip RL entirely and rely only on supervised fine-tuning
Use a single giant environment shared across all task domains
questions.explanation: Orchard trains agents inside real deployment harnesses like Codex, OpenClaw, and ZeroClaw, rather than a separate training-only simulator, so the policy learns the actual tool-calling environment it will run in.

questions.prompt: What happened to Orchard-Claw's score when it was paired with the ZeroClaw deployment system?
options: It dropped from 73.9% to 59.6%
It stayed flat at 59.6%
It rose from 59.6% to 73.9%
It wasn't evaluated with ZeroClaw
questions.explanation: Orchard-Claw scored 59.6% on its own, rising to 73.9% when paired with the ZeroClaw system — showing the deployment harness itself contributes to the result, not just the underlying model.

questions.prompt: What does Orchard Env's infrastructure benchmark show?
options: It launched 1,000 sandboxes in parallel in 26 seconds
It requires no container orchestration at all
It only supports a single fixed base image
It takes several minutes to boot each sandbox
questions.explanation: Microsoft reported Orchard Env launching 1,000 isolated sandboxes in parallel in 26 seconds, with an average 0.28s command-execution latency — the Kubernetes-native layer is built for RL-scale throughput.

posts.title: Gemini Robotics 2: One Reasoning Model, Many Robot Bodies
posts.subtitle: A cloud brain, an on-device brain, and a hard line on where neither is allowed to run.
posts.summary: Google DeepMind shipped Gemini Robotics 2 in July 2026 as a family of models rather than one release: Gemini Robotics 2 (VLA) for turning perception and instructions into robot actions, Gemini Robotics ER 2 for embodied reasoning (built on Gemini 3.5 Flash, 128K input / 64K output), and Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 for running locally without a cloud connection.

slides.title: A Robot 'Brain' Meant to Move Between Bodies
slides.body: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2, published July 2026, splits robot intelligence into three cooperating models instead of one monolithic policy per robot.

slides.title: Robot Policies Traditionally Don't Transfer
bullets: A control policy trained for one robot arm or humanoid historically has to be substantially retrained for a different body — different joints, cameras, and grippers break the mapping from perception to action.
Cloud-only inference adds latency that's a real problem for physical manipulation, where a slow reaction can mean a dropped object or worse.
Giving a robot more autonomy raises a sharper safety question than a chatbot ever does: an unsafe action has physical consequences, not just a bad text output.

slides.title: Three Models, Three Jobs
bullets: Gemini Robotics ER 2 is a vision-language model for embodied reasoning — spatial, temporal, and physical understanding, tool orchestration, and success detection. It's built directly on Gemini 3.5 Flash, taking interleaved text/image/video/audio input up to a 128K context window and producing up to 64K output tokens.
Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 is a vision-language-action model that runs locally on the robot itself — no cloud round-trip — turning camera images and task descriptions straight into control commands.
Both are trained on Google TPUs using the JAX and ML Pathways stack, and ship through Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, and a private-preview Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

slides.title: Cloud Reasoning vs. On-Device Action
bullets: ER 2 is the 'thinking' layer — it reasons about the scene and can call tools — while On-Device 2 is built to execute without waiting on a network connection.
The On-Device model's card describes adapting across different robot hardware through flexible input/output configuration with minimal retraining, rather than a fresh training run per robot.

rows: Spatial/temporal/physical reasoning, tool orchestration, success detection
On the robot, no cloud dependency

slides.title: Whole-Body Control, Demonstrated on a Real Humanoid
bullets: Google DeepMind demonstrated whole-body control running on an Apptronik humanoid robot as part of the announcement, showing the same model family handling coordinated, multi-limb movement rather than a single arm in isolation.

The reasoning model (ER 2) handles 'what should happen next and is it safe,' while the action model executes the movement — a division of labor closer to how a person separates judgment from motor control.

slides.title: Explicitly Off-Limits, By Google's Own Model Card

slides.title: The Bigger Shift: Robotics Intelligence as a Reusable Layer
bullets: Splitting reasoning (ER 2) from action (VLA / On-Device) mirrors a pattern already common in software agents — a 'planner' model and an 'executor' — now applied to physical robots.
Building ER 2 directly on top of Gemini 3.5 Flash means robotics reasoning inherits general-model upgrades instead of needing a from-scratch retrain every cycle.
The explicit, written exclusion of safety-critical domains is a rare case of a lab drawing a hard boundary in the model card itself, not just in marketing language.

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Adding a Node Without Reshuffling Everything
posts.subtitle: The ring trick that keeps distributed caches from stampeding on every scale-out.
posts.summary: Naive hash(key) % N routing remaps almost every key when a node joins or leaves, causing a cache stampede on the backing store. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring so only about 1/N of keys move per node change — and virtual nodes fix the uneven load that a plain ring still produces.

slides.title: The Scaling Move That Shouldn't Empty Your Cache
slides.body: Consistent hashing is the technique behind Cassandra, DynamoDB, and memcached's ketama client: it lets a distributed cache or database add or remove a node while remapping only a small fraction of keys.

slides.title: hash(key) % N Breaks Every Time N Changes
bullets: The obvious way to shard N cache nodes is node = hash(key) % N — simple, and evenly distributed as long as N never changes.
The moment a node is added or removed, N changes, and the modulo of almost every key flips to a different node.
The result is a cache stampede: nearly all keys miss at once and every one of those requests falls through to the backing database simultaneously.

slides.title: Put Nodes and Keys on the Same Ring
bullets: Hash both node identifiers and keys into the same numeric space, and imagine that space bent into a circle (a 'ring').
Each node occupies one point on the ring; a key belongs to whichever node is the next one clockwise from the key's own hash position.
Adding a node only affects the keys between it and the previous node on the ring — every other key's owner is unchanged, because nothing else on the ring moved.

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Ring's Real Weakness
bullets: A plain ring with only a handful of nodes places them unevenly by chance — one node can end up owning a much bigger arc (and much more traffic) than another.

The fix: give each physical node many points on the ring (virtual nodes, often 100-200 per node) instead of one. Load balances out because each physical node's total ring coverage is now an average over many small arcs.
Virtual nodes are why Cassandra and DynamoDB both use this scheme underneath their partitioning — without it, hot physical nodes are common at small cluster sizes.

slides.title: Modulo Hashing vs. Consistent Hashing
bullets: The gap widens as N grows: going from 10 nodes to 11 remaps ~91% of keys under mod-N, versus roughly 9% on a consistent-hash ring.

rows: Even, but only while N is fixed
Even with virtual nodes; skewed without them
Ring position lookup, usually a sorted structure

slides.title: A 4-Node Ring Gains a 5th Node
bullets: Picture 4 nodes placed on a ring at roughly the 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75% marks, each owning the quarter-arc clockwise up to the next node.

Add a 5th node at the 60% mark: it only takes over the keys that used to belong to the node at 50% (the arc from 50% to 60%) — about 1/5 of that one node's former keys, not a fifth of the whole dataset.
The other three nodes never see a single key move — their arcs of the ring are untouched, so their cache entries stay valid and warm.

slides.title: What Consistent Hashing Doesn't Solve
bullets: It only decides ownership, not replication — systems still need a separate strategy (e.g., 'own the next R nodes clockwise') to store copies for fault tolerance.
Keys that remap still require an actual data transfer to the new owner — consistent hashing shrinks how many keys move, it doesn't make moving them free.

For extremely skewed key popularity (a handful of keys getting most of the traffic), even a perfectly balanced ring can leave one node hot — that needs request-level load balancing, not just key placement.
Rendezvous hashing (highest random weight) solves the same remapping problem without maintaining a ring structure at all, and is simpler to reason about for small clusters.

slides.title: When to Reach for This
bullets: Use consistent hashing whenever nodes in a sharded cache or store will scale up or down while it's serving traffic — that's exactly the case where mod-N hashing hurts most.
Always pair it with virtual nodes in practice; a bare ring with few physical nodes routinely produces 2-3x load imbalance.
It's a placement strategy, not a full replication or consistency solution — real systems like Cassandra layer replication and quorum reads/writes on top of the ring.

questions.prompt: With plain hash(key) % N sharding, what happens when a node is added?
options: Nothing remaps, since hashing is stable
Only the new node's keys are affected
Nearly every key's owner changes because N changed
Only keys starting with a specific prefix move
questions.explanation: Because the modulo divisor N changes, almost every key's hash % N result changes too, so nearly all keys remap to a different node at once — the exact stampede consistent hashing avoids.

questions.prompt: In consistent hashing, roughly what fraction of keys move when one node is added to a ring of N nodes?
options: All of them
About 1/N
Exactly half
None, ever
questions.explanation: Only the keys in the arc between the new node and its counter-clockwise neighbor move — roughly a 1/N share of the ring, not the whole keyspace.

questions.prompt: What problem do virtual nodes solve?
options: They replace the need for hashing entirely
They uneven load caused by a few physical nodes landing unevenly on the ring
They eliminate the need for replication
They make hash computation faster
questions.explanation: Giving each physical node many points on the ring averages out the luck of the draw in node placement, so load balances across physical nodes instead of one getting a disproportionately large arc.

posts.title: AskChem: Rebuild Chemistry Search Around Claims
posts.subtitle: One sourced fact per query, not forty PDFs to skim.
posts.summary: AskChem rebuilds chemistry literature search around atomic, DOI-grounded claims instead of ranked papers, linking 2.4M claims through a 171K-edge evidence graph with 97.9% expert-audited precision. It ships a web UI, SDK, and MCP server on the same claim store — built for agents to query, not just humans to browse.

slides.title: The Paper Isn't the Answer — the Claim Inside It Is
slides.body: AskChem, the #1 trending paper on Hugging Face Daily Papers, rebuilds chemistry literature search around atomic, DOI-grounded claims instead of ranked documents.

slides.title: Ranked Documents Don't Answer Cross-Paper Questions
bullets: A question like 'which solvents give the highest yield for this reaction class' needs facts scattered across dozens of separate papers.
Standard literature search returns a ranked list of PDFs — a scientist, or an AI agent, still has to open each one, find the fact, and verify where it came from.
Provenance is the hard part in chemistry: an unsourced or wrong number can send a real experiment down the wrong path.

slides.title: Retrieve Claims, Not Papers
bullets: Each paper is decomposed into atomic, typed claims — every claim grounded by a source DOI plus a verbatim quote or explicit evidence locator.
A shared claim store powers two structures on top: a stabilized faceted taxonomy for hierarchical browsing, and an evidence graph linking claims to each other through typed relations.
An exploratory 'living taxonomy' situates papers under scientific principles rather than journal categories.

slides.title: One Claim Store, Three Access Points
bullets: The deployed service indexes 2.4M claims, 307K taxonomy nodes, and 171K evidence edges.
The web interface, an SDK, and an MCP server all query the same REST schema — an agent gets the identical claim graph a human researcher browses.

slides.title: 97.9% Precision, Measured by Domain Experts
bullets: AskChem-Bench specifically probes condition aggregation, temporal tracking, and contradiction surfacing — multi-paper reasoning ranked search can't do.

slides.title: A Worked Query: "What's Changed About This Catalyst Since 2020?"
bullets: Ranked search returns 40 papers mentioning the catalyst; a researcher would skim each one for a claim about performance over time.

AskChem instead pulls every typed claim tagged to that catalyst, orders them by publication date via their DOIs, and surfaces evidence-graph edges where later claims contradict or refine earlier ones.
The answer arrives as a chain of sourced claims, not a list of PDFs to re-read.

slides.title: Where the Claim Store Still Has Gaps
bullets: The authors don't yet isolate how much retrieval quality comes specifically from the taxonomy versus other signals in the hybrid ranker.
The 'living taxonomy' is explicitly exploratory — no claim of expert-validated placement of papers under scientific principles.

Claim extraction inherits LLM extraction errors: a claim's phrasing can drift from the source even when its DOI/quote link is correct, so the evidence locator — not the claim text alone — is the ground truth.

slides.title: Why This Matters Beyond Chemistry
bullets: Claim-level, provenance-grounded retrieval is a template other 'AI agent reads the literature' systems will likely copy — RAG over papers, not RAG over paragraphs.
Shipping an MCP server alongside the web UI and SDK on day one is notable: it's built to be an agent's tool, not just a human's search box.
97.9% edge precision came from a human audit, not a benchmark leaderboard — claim graphs still need expert QA, they don't self-verify.

questions.explanation: AskChem converts each paper into atomic, typed claims, each grounded by a source DOI and a verbatim quote or evidence locator — that claim, not the paper, is what gets retrieved and linked.

questions.explanation: A domain-expert audit estimated 97.9% edge-type precision on the evidence graph — a human-verified number, not an automated proxy metric.

options: Released any code or benchmark

questions.explanation: The paper is upfront about its limits: it doesn't isolate the taxonomy's specific contribution to retrieval, and the 'living taxonomy' placements haven't been expert-validated — it's exploratory, not a finished ontology.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: A Server Pausing to Ask the Human
posts.subtitle: The fourth MCP primitive — for when the model genuinely doesn't know.
posts.summary: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-tool-call and request structured input from the human, through the client, without needing its own UI. It's the fourth primitive alongside Sampling, Roots, and Authorization — and the spec is strict about what it can and can't be used to ask for.

slides.title: Sometimes the Right Move Is to Ask
slides.body: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-tool-call and request structured input from the human — through the client, without needing its own UI.

slides.title: A Tool Call That Needs Info Nobody Passed In
bullets: A booking-agent MCP server gets called with a destination but no travel dates — the model either guesses, the call fails, or the developer pre-builds a rigid form for every possible gap.
Before elicitation, an MCP server had no protocol-native way to ask the human directly; it could only return an error or a best-effort default back to the model.

slides.title: The Server Sends elicitation/create, the Client Renders It
bullets: Mid-execution, the server sends an elicitation/create request carrying a requestedSchema — a restricted subset of JSON Schema: flat, primitive fields only (strings, numbers, enums, booleans).
The client, not the server, renders the actual form or prompt, collects the human's answer, and returns it as structured, schema-validated data.
Execution resumes inside the same tool call with real input, instead of the model hallucinating a plausible-sounding default.

slides.title: Two Elicitation Modes: Form and URL
bullets: Form mode: the client renders the schema as an in-place form for ordinary structured input — pick a date, choose a seat class, confirm a count.
URL mode, added in the 2026-07-28 spec, instead redirects the user to an external URL — for interactions sensitive enough that they must never pass through the MCP client at all.

slides.title: Concrete Flow: Booking a Flight
bullets: Model calls book_flight(destination: 'Tokyo') with no dates. The server's requestedSchema needs departDate and returnDate as ISO date strings.
The client shows the human a date picker; they pick Aug 20 - Aug 27. The client sends that back as the elicitation response.
The server validates it against its own schema, then actually books — the model never had to invent or confirm dates itself.

slides.title: Elicitation vs. the Other MCP Primitives
bullets: Elicitation is the only one of the four aimed at the human, not the model or the filesystem — a UI hook the protocol standardizes so every client renders it consistently.

rows: Server borrows the client's LLM to reason
Client tells server which filesystem paths it may touch
Server asks the human a direct question mid-call

slides.title: Why You Can't Elicit a Password
bullets: The spec is explicit: servers MUST NOT use form-mode elicitation for passwords, API keys, access tokens, or payment credentials — the client isn't a guaranteed-confidential channel end-to-end.
Every round trip pauses the tool call on a human response — fine for a one-off booking, wrong for a high-frequency batch job or anything meant to run unattended.
Over-eliciting trains users to click through prompts without reading them, the same fatigue problem as OS permission dialogs — ask only for what the model genuinely can't infer or default.

slides.title: The Fourth Pillar of MCP's Client-Server Contract
bullets: Sampling lets a server borrow reasoning, Roots lets it borrow a filesystem boundary, Authorization lets it borrow trust — Elicitation lets it borrow a moment of the human's attention.
Use it for genuinely missing, human-only information — a choice, a confirmation, a date — not as a substitute for a well-designed tool schema.
URL mode exists precisely so 'sensitive' and 'elicitable' don't have to be the same category forever.

questions.prompt: What does an MCP server send to start an elicitation?
options: A sampling/createMessage request
An elicitation/create request with a requestedSchema
A roots/list request
An OAuth token
questions.explanation: The server sends elicitation/create carrying a requestedSchema — a restricted JSON Schema — so the client knows exactly what shape of answer to collect.

questions.prompt: Why can't a server use form-mode elicitation to ask for a password?
options: Passwords aren't valid JSON Schema types
The spec prohibits it — the client isn't a guaranteed-confidential channel for that data
Elicitation only accepts numbers
Servers can't send text fields
questions.explanation: The spec explicitly bars form-mode elicitation for passwords, API keys, tokens, and payment credentials; URL mode exists for exactly this kind of sensitive interaction instead.

questions.prompt: Which MCP primitive is elicitation most different from in purpose?
options: Sampling — because it targets the human, not the model
Roots — because it also uses JSON Schema
Authorization — because both are optional
Nothing, they all do the same job
questions.explanation: Sampling has the server borrow the client's LLM; elicitation instead pauses execution to ask a human directly — the two primitives route the same kind of gap to completely different actors.

posts.title: Decoding Strategies: How an LLM Actually Picks Its Words
posts.subtitle: Temperature, top-k, and top-p aren't three separate settings — they're one filter chain applied in sequence
posts.summary: An LLM outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary for every token, not a single answer. Decoding strategies decide how that distribution turns into an actual word: temperature reshapes it, top-k/top-p/min-p cut off the unreliable tail, and only then does sampling happen. Get the combination wrong and you get either robotic repetition or confident nonsense.

slides.title: Every Generated Word Is a Dice Roll You Can Rig
slides.body: An LLM doesn't 'decide' what to say next — it outputs a probability over its entire vocabulary, and a decoding strategy picks one token from that distribution. Temperature, top-k, and top-p are the knobs that shape which dice you're rolling.

slides.title: Greedy Decoding Is Fast but Predictably Boring
bullets: Always picking the single highest-probability token (greedy / argmax) is deterministic and cheap, but produces repetitive, generic text — the same phrasing every time

Pure random sampling from the full distribution goes too far the other way: with 50k-100k+ tokens in the vocabulary, the long tail includes genuinely bad next tokens that occasionally get picked, producing incoherent output
Neither extreme is usable in production — you need to keep some randomness for variety without ever sampling from the garbage tail

slides.title: Temperature Reshapes the Distribution Before You Sample
slides.body: Temperature (T) divides the logits before the softmax: softmax(logits / T). T < 1 sharpens the distribution toward the top tokens; T > 1 flattens it toward uniform; T = 1 leaves it unchanged.
bullets: T → 0: distribution collapses toward argmax — effectively greedy, deterministic, repetitive
T ≈ 0.7-0.9: common production default — enough sharpening to stay coherent, enough spread to vary across calls
T > 1.2: the distribution flattens enough that low-probability, often nonsensical tokens become live options — output visibly degrades
Temperature alone never removes bad tokens from consideration — it only reweights every token's odds, including the terrible ones

slides.title: Top-k, Top-p, and Min-p Actually Cut Off the Tail
bullets: Top-k: keep only the k highest-probability tokens, zero out the rest, renormalize, then sample — simple, but a fixed k is the wrong size for both very peaked and very flat distributions

Top-p (nucleus sampling): sort tokens by probability and keep adding them until cumulative probability crosses p (e.g. 0.9), then sample only from that set — the set size adapts per step instead of staying fixed
Min-p: keep tokens whose probability is at least p times the top token's probability — scales directly with how confident the model is at that step
These are filters applied AFTER temperature scaling, not instead of it — a real request stacks temperature, then a cutoff rule, then samples

slides.title: Worked Example: One Distribution, Four Outcomes
slides.body: Prompt: 'The capital of France is'. Say the model's next-token probabilities look like: Paris 0.62, a 0.15, located 0.08, definitely 0.06, and a long tail of ~50k other tokens sharing the remaining 0.09.
bullets: Greedy (T→0): always outputs "Paris" — correct, but zero variation across repeated calls
T=1, top-p=0.9: nucleus = {Paris, a, located, definitely} (cumulative ≈0.91) — every sample lands on a sensible continuation
T=1, no cutoff: the full tail stays in play, so roughly 9% of calls sample from that ~50k-token tail — occasional non-sequiturs
T=1.5, no cutoff: flattening makes that unsafe tail even more likely to get picked — visibly worse coherence

rows: ~9% chance of a low-probability, odd token
Flattened distribution makes that tail even likelier

slides.title: Top-k vs Top-p vs Min-p

rows: Yes — nucleus shrinks or grows per step
Too small on flat distributions, too large on peaked ones
Can still admit a long tail when probabilities are nearly flat

slides.title: When Defaults Bite You
bullets: Setting temperature=0 in most APIs doesn't guarantee identical output across calls — floating-point non-determinism and batching on the server side can still cause small variation
Combining aggressive settings (high temperature AND high top-p AND no top-k) removes every safety net at once — that's when generation goes off the rails
For reliability-critical tasks (function calling, structured JSON, code), use low temperature and a tight top-p; for creative writing or brainstorming, open both up
Repetition/frequency penalty is a separate mechanism — it penalizes tokens already used in the output, not the per-step distribution shape. Don't confuse it with temperature or top-p

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Decoding = reshape the distribution (temperature) → cut off the tail (top-k / top-p / min-p) → sample
Lower temperature and tighter cutoffs for correctness-critical tasks; higher and looser for creative variety
Top-p adapts to the model's per-step confidence in a way a fixed top-k can't — it's the more common production default today
None of these settings change what the model 'knows' — they only change how much randomness you let it express

questions.prompt: What does temperature actually do to the model's output probabilities?
options: It removes low-probability tokens from consideration entirely
It divides the logits before the softmax, sharpening (T<1) or flattening (T>1) the distribution
It only affects the first token generated
It retrains the model's weights for that request
questions.explanation: Temperature rescales logits before softmax — it never deletes tokens, it just reweights every token's relative odds. Cutting off unlikely tokens entirely is a separate job, done by top-k, top-p, or min-p.

questions.prompt: Why does top-p (nucleus sampling) often beat a fixed top-k in practice?
options: It's cheaper to compute
Its candidate set size adapts to the model's confidence at each step, instead of always keeping exactly k tokens
It guarantees fully deterministic output
It doesn't require sorting the probabilities
questions.explanation: Top-k always keeps the same number of candidates no matter how peaked or flat the distribution is. Top-p keeps growing the candidate set only until cumulative probability crosses p, so it naturally shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it's uncertain.

questions.prompt: You're building a function-calling agent that must output valid, parseable JSON. Which decoding setup fits best?
options: High temperature, high top-p, no top-k — maximize creativity
Low temperature and a tight top-p — minimize randomness so output stays consistent and parseable
Temperature is irrelevant to JSON validity
Always use the highest available temperature regardless of task
questions.explanation: Reliability-critical tasks like structured extraction or function calling want low variance: low temperature plus a tight top-p keeps sampling close to the model's most confident path, reducing the chance a stray token derails the format.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Context-Free Chunks
posts.subtitle: A short LLM-written blurb per chunk can cut retrieval failures by up to two-thirds
posts.summary: Chunking a document for RAG strips away the surrounding context each chunk needs to be found. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by having an LLM prepend a short, chunk-specific summary before embedding and keyword-indexing — and prompt caching keeps the cost low enough to run over an entire corpus.

slides.title: Your chunks forgot what document they're from
slides.body: Split a 50-page filing into 200-token chunks and most of them read like orphaned sentences. Embeddings can only match what's on the page — and a page that says 'revenue grew 3%' with no company or quarter attached is nearly unsearchable.

slides.title: Chunking trades recall for indexability
slides.body: You chunk because embedding a whole document blurs it into a mushy average vector that matches everything and nothing. But small chunks lose the referents — pronouns, company names, dates, section headers — that a query actually searches on.
bullets: A chunk reading 'the company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' has no company, no year, no filing type
Standard fixes — bigger chunks, sliding windows, overlap — trade the same problem for a blurrier one
The failure is silent: retrieval just returns the wrong top-k, and nothing in the pipeline flags it

slides.title: Prepend context before you index, not after you retrieve
slides.body: For every chunk, an LLM reads the chunk alongside the full source document and writes a 1-2 sentence blurb that situates it — then that blurb is glued onto the chunk before it goes into both the embedding index and the keyword (BM25) index.
bullets: Prompt: 'here is the whole document; here is one chunk from it; write brief context to situate this chunk for search retrieval'
The generated context is prepended, not appended — it becomes part of what gets embedded
It also gets indexed into BM25, so exact keyword matches (part numbers, tickers, names) improve too, not just semantic ones

slides.title: Prompt caching is what makes this affordable
slides.body: Naively, re-contextualizing every chunk means re-sending the whole document once per chunk — a document with 100 chunks gets read 100 times. Caching the document as a shared prefix and only varying the chunk in each call turns that into one long-context read plus 100 cheap cache hits.
bullets: Without caching: cost scales with (chunks × document length) — expensive for long documents
With prompt caching: the document is written to cache once, each chunk-context call reuses it near-free
Anthropic reported roughly $1.02 per million document tokens processed this way — cheap enough to run over a full corpus, not just a sample

slides.title: Each layer you add compounds the gain
slides.body: Anthropic's own eval (top-20 chunk retrieval failure rate, averaged across several codebases and knowledge bases) showed the gains stack rather than substitute for each other.

slides.title: Same sentence, before and after
slides.body: The chunk's raw text never changes — you're not summarizing it away, you're wrapping it.
bullets: Raw chunk: 'The company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter.'
Generated context: 'This chunk is from an SEC filing on ACME Corp's Q2 2023 performance; the previous quarter refers to Q1 2023.'
Indexed text: context + raw chunk — now a query for 'ACME Q2 2023 revenue growth' has real terms to match on, in both the vector index and BM25

slides.title: Where it doesn't pay off
slides.body: This is an indexing-time cost for a retrieval-time gain — it's the wrong trade in a few cases.
bullets: Small corpora that already fit in a single context window: skip retrieval entirely, just stuff the whole thing in the prompt
Highly dynamic corpora: every edit means re-contextualizing and re-indexing affected chunks, so update-heavy stores pay this cost repeatedly
Cheap or low-quality context-generation prompts produce generic blurbs ('this chunk discusses financial results') that add tokens without adding signal — the context has to actually be specific
It improves recall, not reasoning — a retrieval system that finds the right chunk but hands it to a weak generator still produces a weak answer

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Chunking for RAG throws away the context a chunk needs to be found — contextual retrieval writes that context back in before indexing
It touches both indexes: contextual embeddings for semantic match, contextual BM25 for exact keyword match
Prompt caching is the enabler — without it, re-reading the full document per chunk makes this too expensive to run at corpus scale
Stack it with reranking for the largest combined gain; each layer addresses a different failure mode
Best fit for large, relatively stable corpora where retrieval quality — not update latency — is the bottleneck

questions.prompt: What does contextual retrieval actually change about a chunk before it's indexed?
options: It shortens the chunk to remove redundant words
It prepends a short LLM-generated blurb that situates the chunk within its source document
It translates the chunk into a canonical schema
It replaces the chunk's text with its embedding vector
questions.explanation: The raw chunk text is preserved; a short situating blurb (e.g. which document, company, time period) is generated and prepended, then both pieces are indexed together — into the embedding index and the BM25 keyword index.

questions.prompt: Why is prompt caching essential to making this technique practical?
options: It makes the embedding model faster at query time
It avoids re-sending the full source document on every single chunk's context-generation call
It compresses the vector index to save storage
It lets you skip generating context for short chunks
questions.explanation: Without caching, generating context for every chunk means resending the whole document each time — cost scales with chunks × document length. Caching the document once as a shared prefix turns that into one full read plus cheap cache hits per chunk.

questions.prompt: Based on the reported failure-rate numbers, which combination produced the largest reduction over baseline embeddings?
options: Contextual embeddings alone (-35%)
Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 (-49%)
Contextual embeddings + BM25 + reranking (-67%)
BM25 alone, no embeddings
questions.explanation: The gains compound: contextual embeddings cut the failure rate by 35%, adding contextual BM25 brought it to 49%, and stacking a reranking step on top brought the combined reduction to 67% versus the embeddings-only baseline.
