posts.title: Prompt Caching: Paying Full Price to Re-Read the Same Prefix
posts.subtitle: Why re-sending an identical 40K-token system prompt on every turn is the most avoidable cost in an LLM app
posts.summary: Prompt caching reuses a model's stored key/value activations for a prefix that hasn't changed, so a repeated system prompt or tool schema gets skipped instead of reprocessed. It turns cost and latency from scaling with total prompt length into scaling with just the new tokens — but only if the prefix matches byte-for-byte and you reuse it inside the cache's TTL.

slides.title: You're Paying to Re-Read the Same Prompt Every Turn
slides.body: A coding agent that ships a 40,000-token system prompt with every request pays for those 40,000 tokens again on turn two, turn three, and every turn after — even though nothing in them changed.

slides.title: Every Call Reprocesses the Full Prompt From Token Zero
slides.body: A transformer computes attention over every token in the input, every single call. Without caching, the model has no memory that it already saw this exact prefix a second ago.
bullets: A support bot with a 30K-token policy doc + tool schema pays for those 30K tokens on every one of 10,000 daily requests
Cost and latency scale with total prompt length, not with the handful of new tokens the user actually added
Multi-turn agents resend the entire growing transcript each turn — the waste compounds as the conversation gets longer

slides.title: Cache the KV Activations for a Prefix, Not the Text
slides.body: The first call computes and stores the key/value activations for a prefix. Any later call whose prompt starts with that identical prefix skips recomputing attention for those tokens and processes only what's new.
bullets: Providers let you mark 'cache breakpoints' — points in the prompt (end of system instructions, end of tool defs) up to which the prefix should be cached
The match is exact and positional: caching operates on the literal token sequence from position zero, not on meaning or similarity
A cache hit means the model only runs the expensive forward pass on the suffix — the new user turn

slides.title: Cache Reads Are Cheap; Cache Writes Cost a Bit More
slides.body: Every major provider prices a cache write above the base input rate and a cache read well below it — the discount is the entire incentive to restructure your prompt around a stable prefix.

rows: explicit caches: minutes to hours, set by you

slides.title: Worked Example: A Support Agent's Per-Turn Bill
slides.body: Say the shared prefix (system prompt + tool schemas + policy doc) is 40,000 tokens and each user turn adds 200 new tokens.
bullets: Uncached: every turn reprocesses all 40,200 tokens — cost and latency stay flat and high no matter how short the actual question is

Cached: turn one writes the 40,000-token prefix to cache (paying the write premium); turn two through N, while inside the TTL, reprocess only the 200 new tokens at the discounted cache-read rate on the 40,000
The saving grows with how many turns land inside one TTL window — one-off single-shot calls barely benefit, since they only ever pay the write price

slides.title: The Prefix Has to Match Exactly — and the Clock Is Ticking
slides.body: Prompt caching is a positional-match optimization, not a semantic one, and that makes it easy to accidentally defeat.
bullets: Any edit before the cache breakpoint — a reordered few-shot example, an injected timestamp, a different tool listed first — invalidates the cache for everything after it
Put stable content (instructions, tool defs, examples) first and volatile content (the live user turn) last, or you'll never get a hit
If traffic doesn't reuse the same prefix again before the TTL expires, you only ever pay the more expensive write price and never recoup it
Caching a prefix stuffed with per-user IDs or live data wastes the discount — cache what's actually shared across calls

slides.title: Order Your Prompt for the Cache, Then Measure It
slides.body: Prompt caching turns per-call cost from O(total prompt length) into roughly O(new tokens) — but only for prefixes that are stable and actually get reused.
bullets: Structure prompts static-first, dynamic-last: system prompt → tools → few-shot examples → (cache breakpoint) → live conversation
Track cache hit rate as a first-class metric alongside latency and cost — a low hit rate usually means something upstream keeps changing the prefix
It's a free win for high-volume agents and chat apps with a large shared context; it's close to useless for single, one-off completions

questions.prompt: What determines whether a prompt-caching cache hit occurs on a new request?
options: The new prompt has similar meaning to a previous one
The new prompt's prefix matches a previously cached prefix exactly, token-for-token, from the start
The request uses the same API key as before
The model's temperature setting is unchanged
questions.explanation: Caching is a positional, exact-match optimization on the token sequence — not a semantic one. Editing anything before the cache breakpoint, even a timestamp, invalidates the cache for every token after it.

questions.prompt: Why does prompt caching mainly pay off for high-volume agents with a large shared prefix, rather than one-off single questions?
options: Caching is technically disabled for short prompts
The first call pays a premium to write the cache, so only repeated reuse of that prefix within the TTL earns the discount back
Cache reads are billed at full price regardless of hits
One-off questions aren't allowed to use cached prefixes at all
questions.explanation: A cache write typically costs more than a normal input token. A single call that never gets reused only ever pays that premium — the savings only materialize once later calls hit the cache within its TTL.

questions.prompt: You have a 40K-token system prompt and want to maximize cache hits across turns. Where should the volatile, per-turn user message go relative to the cache breakpoint?
options: Before the stable content, so it's processed first
Interleaved throughout the stable content for balance
After the stable content and the cache breakpoint, since anything before the breakpoint must stay identical
It doesn't matter where it goes
questions.explanation: Because the match is positional and exact, only content before the cache breakpoint needs to stay identical across calls. Put static content (system prompt, tools, examples) first, and the changing user turn last.

posts.title: Activity Frames: Replay a Task Instead of Re-Deriving It
posts.subtitle: A deterministic compiler turns a day of screen activity into workflows an agent can run at near-zero token cost
posts.summary: Activity Frames compiles raw screen recordings into deterministic, agent-executable 'frames' instead of feeding raw pixels to an LLM. Computer-use agents stop re-deriving the same repetitive task from scratch and instead replay a compiled workflow, cutting token cost on the happy path to near zero.

slides.title: Your agent forgets what you did five minutes ago
slides.body: Every new conversation with a computer-use agent starts blind — it doesn't know what you already did today, and it re-reasons through tasks it has already solved dozens of times.

slides.title: Two failures, one root cause: no persistent activity record
slides.body: Computer-use agents burn tokens re-deriving repetitive tasks from scratch, and they start every session with zero awareness of what the user did between conversations.
bullets: Repetitive tasks (same LinkedIn outreach, same weekly report) get fully re-reasoned every single time
Agents have no grounded record of prior screen activity — no memory of apps used, sites visited, or steps taken
Feeding raw screen video to an LLM for this is expensive and non-deterministic

slides.title: A three-stage, deterministic pipeline — no LLM in the loop
slides.body: Capture, Compilation, and Serving are cleanly separated, and the compiler stage is 100% deterministic: same input always produces the same frame.
bullets: Capture: screen snapshots + accessibility-tree data + input events stream into local SQLite storage
Compilation: sessionizes activity, detects dwell periods and gaps, merges flicker, types entities via 25+ site parsers — using on-device OCR only, no remote model calls
Serving: an MCP server exposes six tools — get_context, get_activity, get_steps, get_day_summary, get_patterns, get_communications

slides.title: Tier 1 facts vs. Tier 2 inference — a hard contract
slides.body: Every frame enforces a two-tier honesty contract so an agent never mistakes a guess for a fact.
bullets: Tier 1: only measurable, deterministically-derived facts — app name, site, timestamps, duration, click/key counts
Tier 2 (optional): any inferred label gets tagged with an explicit confidence level, never presented as ground truth
Every frame keeps evidence pointers back to the raw capture rows it was built from

slides.title: Worked example: a LinkedIn outreach message, replayed not re-reasoned
slides.body: A messaging workflow performed once becomes a reusable, executable script.
bullets: The compiler reduces the demonstrated task to ordered operations — focus, click, type — grounded by element name and role
Next time, the agent slots in a new recipient and new message text, then replays the script instead of re-deriving the steps
Roughly 342 minutes of a day's raw activity compresses to about 150 words of context — and a full day compiles in under one second

slides.title: Re-deriving vs. replaying a known task
slides.body: The paper's core metric, Routine Overhead Ratio, measures exactly this gap across weeks of real activity.

rows: Under 1 second for a full day

slides.title: Where it breaks down
slides.body: This only helps with tasks the user has already performed — and it trades some setup complexity for that speedup.
bullets: Genuinely novel, first-time tasks have no prior frame to replay — the agent is back to full reasoning
Unknown or unlisted websites fall back to generic references instead of rich, typed entities (25+ sites get full parsing, the long tail doesn't)
Local-only by design: typed text capture is opt-in (--include-text) and audio is off by default, so some workflows need explicit consent flags
v0.2, tested primarily on Apple Silicon macOS — the Intel build exists but is less exercised

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Deterministic compilation, not another model call, is what makes agent memory cheap and trustworthy.
bullets: Separating capture, deterministic compilation, and MCP serving keeps the expensive part (LLM reasoning) out of the memory pipeline entirely
The Tier 1 / Tier 2 fact-vs-inference split is a reusable pattern for any agent memory system that wants to avoid hallucinated context
Replay only pays off for repeated work — pair it with normal reasoning for anything the user hasn't done before

questions.prompt: What is the main problem Activity Frames is designed to solve?
options: Slow screen recording performance on older hardware
Agents re-deriving repetitive tasks from scratch and lacking a record of what the user already did
LLMs being unable to read accessibility trees
A lack of open-source screen recording software
questions.explanation: The paper targets two linked failures: agents burning tokens re-reasoning through tasks they've already performed, and agents starting each session blind to prior user activity.

questions.prompt: Why does the compilation stage use no LLM calls?
options: LLMs are too slow to run locally
To keep compilation deterministic and cheap — the same capture data always produces the same frame
Because the accessibility tree cannot be read by language models
To comply with app store policies
questions.explanation: Compilation relies on on-device OCR and rule-based sessionizing/entity-typing instead of a model, so the same input reliably produces the same output — a property replay depends on.

questions.prompt: What does the Tier 1 / Tier 2 distinction protect against?
options: Running out of disk space
Presenting an inferred or guessed label as if it were a measured fact
Exceeding the MCP server's rate limit
Losing data if the recording app crashes
questions.explanation: Tier 1 holds only directly measurable facts (timestamps, click counts, app names); Tier 2 holds inferences, always tagged with a confidence level, so downstream agents can tell a fact from a guess.

posts.title: Chunking Strategies: The RAG Decision Nobody Profiles
posts.subtitle: How you split a document decides what your retriever can ever find — before the embedding model gets a vote
posts.summary: Chunking — how a document gets split before embedding — sets a hard ceiling on retrieval quality that no downstream model can fix. Fixed-size, structure-aware, semantic, and sentence-window chunking each trade off simplicity, coherence, and ingest cost differently, and picking wrong shows up as silent recall failures, not errors.

slides.title: The retrieval bug that never throws an exception
slides.body: Teams tune embedding models and rerankers for weeks while the actual ceiling on recall was set at ingest time, by how the document got cut into pieces.

slides.title: Fixed-size chunking splits ideas, not just text
slides.body: The simplest approach — cut every N tokens — has no idea where a sentence, clause, or table row actually ends.
bullets: A 512-token window can cut a clause defining a term in half, embedding neither half well
The query 'what is the termination clause' can score low against both halves even though the answer is right there
Recall failures like this are silent: no error, no crash, just a document the retriever should have found and didn't

slides.title: Four common strategies, in order of complexity
slides.body: Each strategy moves the tradeoff between simplicity and semantic coherence.
bullets: Fixed-size + overlap: split every N tokens (commonly 256–512) with ~10–20% overlap so boundary content appears in two chunks
Recursive / structure-aware: split on markdown headers, paragraphs, or sentence boundaries first, falling back to fixed-size only when a section is still too large
Semantic chunking: embed sentences, then cut where consecutive-sentence similarity drops — chunks track topic shifts instead of a token count
Sentence-window retrieval: index single sentences for precise matching, but return a wider window of surrounding text as the actual context

slides.title: Worked example: a 40-page vendor contract
slides.body: The same document, chunked three ways, produces three very different retrieval outcomes for one query.
bullets: Fixed-size (512 tokens, 50-token overlap): the 'Effective Date' clause spans a chunk boundary — a query for it retrieves the wrong half more than a third of the time
Structure-aware (split on section headers like '§4 Termination'): the clause stays intact, retrieval recall jumps because the chunk is exactly the semantic unit a lawyer would also read
Semantic chunking: correctly isolates the clause too, but costs an extra embedding pass over every sentence at ingest time before chunk boundaries are even decided

slides.title: Picking a strategy
slides.body: No single method wins on every axis — pick based on document structure and ingest budget.

rows: Docs with real headings (contracts, docs, wikis)
Dense prose with no clear structure
More moving parts in the pipeline

slides.title: Pitfalls and when to stop tuning this
slides.body: Chunking has diminishing returns past a point, and overlap isn't free.
bullets: Chunks too small (under ~100 tokens): high retrieval noise, and the embedding carries too little context to be distinctive
Chunks too large (over ~1–2k tokens): the query's signal gets diluted by unrelated content in the same chunk, hurting cosine similarity
Overlap multiplies storage and can return near-duplicate chunks in the same result set — dedup downstream or it wastes context budget
If the source is already structured data (a database table, a key-value config), don't chunk it at all — query it directly instead of forcing it through embeddings

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Chunking is a retrieval-quality decision, not a preprocessing detail — treat it with the same rigor as choosing an embedding model.
bullets: Default to structure-aware chunking whenever the source has real headings or sections — it's usually free recall improvement over fixed-size
Reach for semantic chunking only when the ingest cost is worth it — dense, unstructured prose with no natural breakpoints
Always keep some overlap (10–20%) so boundary-spanning facts survive in at least one chunk
Measure recall on real queries before and after a chunking change — it's the cheapest lever in a RAG pipeline and the easiest to get wrong silently

questions.prompt: Why can fixed-size chunking cause a retriever to miss an obviously relevant passage?
options: The embedding model doesn't support long documents
It can split a semantic unit (like a clause or sentence) across two chunks, weakening both embeddings
Fixed-size chunks are always too large to embed
Vector databases reject fixed-size chunks
questions.explanation: Fixed-size chunking ignores content structure, so it can cut a sentence or clause in half — neither resulting chunk embeds the full idea well, which lowers similarity to a relevant query.

questions.prompt: What does semantic chunking use to decide where to cut a document?
options: A fixed token count only
Random sampling of paragraphs
Drops in similarity between consecutive sentence embeddings
The file size in kilobytes
questions.explanation: Semantic chunking embeds sentences and cuts where consecutive-sentence similarity drops sharply, aligning chunk boundaries with actual topic shifts rather than a token count.

questions.prompt: When should you skip chunking and embeddings entirely?
options: When the document is longer than 10 pages
When the source is already structured data, like a database table, that can be queried directly
When the embedding model is expensive
Chunking should never be skipped for RAG
questions.explanation: Structured data like database tables or key-value configs can be queried exactly — forcing it through chunking and embeddings adds cost and imprecision for no benefit.
